Having honored Yājñavalkya, the Lord of Yogins, the sages said:
"Tell us, in their entirety, the duties of those belonging to the castes and stages of life, as well as those outside them."
Remaining in Mithilā, that lord of yogis, having meditated for a moment, spoke to the sages:
"In whatever region there is a black antelope, in that place you should learn the laws of dharma."
The Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, the Dharmaśāstras, and the auxiliary sciences (Aṅgas)—
these, together with the Vedas, are the fourteen seats of knowledge and of dharma.
Manu, Atri, Viṣṇu, Hārīta, Yājñavalkya, Uśanas,
Aṅgiras, Yama, Āpastamba, Saṃvarta, Kātyāyana, and Bṛhaspati.
Parāśara, Vyāsa, Śaṅkha, and Likhita; Dakṣa and Gautama; Śātātapa and Vasiṣṭha—these are the authors of the Dharmaśāstras.
When a gift is given at the proper place, at the proper time, with the right means, and with wealth accompanied by faith,
to a worthy recipient— that is the complete definition of dharma.
Revelation, tradition, the conduct of the virtuous, and what is pleasing to oneself—desire born of right resolve: this is remembered as the root of Dharma.
Among the acts of sacrifice, right conduct, self-control, non-violence, charity, and the study of sacred texts, this indeed is the supreme dharma: the perception of the Self through yoga.
A council (*parṣat*) consists of four who know the Vedas and the Dharma, or even those who possess the threefold knowledge (*traividya*);
whatever that [council] declares shall be the Dharma, or a single person who is the most eminent among those who know the supreme self (*adhyātma*).
[2. The Section on the Religious Student] (p. 5) Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.10: The castes are the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra; however, the first three are the twice-born.
For them, the rites beginning with the impregnation ceremony (*niṣeka*) and ending with the funeral pyre (*śmaśāna*) are indeed performed with sacred mantras.

The conception-rite (*garbhādhāna*) is performed during the fertile period; the male-consecration (*pumsavana*) before the movement of the fetus; the parting-of-the-hair (*sīmantonnayana*) in the sixth or eighth month; and these, along with the birth-rite (*jātakarman*), are to be performed within one month [of birth].
On the eleventh day the naming ceremony is performed; in the fourth month the first outing;
in the sixth month the first feeding of solid food; and the tonsure ceremony should be performed according to family custom.
In this way, the sin arising from seed and womb is pacified;
these rites for women are performed silently, but their marriage is accompanied by mantras.

The initiation of a Brāhmaṇa should take place in the eighth year from conception or in the eighth year from birth; for Kṣatriyas, in the eleventh year, according to some; and for Vaiśyas, in the same year, according to others, or according to family custom.
Having initiated the pupil, the teacher should teach him the Veda preceded by the Great Utterances (mahāvyāhṛtis),
and he should also instruct him in the rules of purification and proper conduct.
During the day and at the twilights, one should void urine and feces with the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) placed over the ear while facing north; if it is at night, one should face south.
Having risen with his penis still held [in the hand],
he should diligently perform purification that removes both odor and residue, using earth and water drawn from a source.
With his knees between his hands, seated in a clean place facing north or east,
a twice-born man should always perform the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśet) using the Brāhma-tīrtha.
The base of the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb, as well as the tip of the hand,
are respectively the *tīrthas* of Prajāpati, the Pitṛs, Brahmā, and the Devas.
Having sipped water three times and wiped [the mouth] twice, one should touch the cavities of the head with water—water that is natural, free from foam and bubbles. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.20)
The twice-born are purified by water reaching the heart, the throat, and the palate, respectively; women and Śūdras are purified when the water merely touches the lips once.
Bathing with mantras dedicated to the waters, sprinkling [the body], restraint of the breath,
worship of the sun, and the daily recitation of the Gāyatrī.
One should recite the Gāyatrī together with its head and preceded by the Vyāhṛtis, joined with the Praṇava at the beginning of each; this threefold repetition is the restraint of breath (prāṇāyāma).
Having restrained his breath and sprinkled himself with water while reciting the three verses addressed to the Waters (*ab-daivata*),
he should sit reciting the *Sāvitrī* until the appearance of the stars in the west.
One should perform the morning twilight ritual in this manner before sunrise, remaining standing until the sun is seen;
thereafter, one should perform the fire-ritual during both twilights.
Then he should salute his elders, saying, "I am [Name]," and he should also attend upon his teacher with a concentrated mind for the sake of Vedic study.
When summoned, he should study; whatever he has obtained, he should report it to him.
He should always act for his benefit through the actions of mind, speech, and body.

Those who are grateful, non-malicious, intelligent, pure, virtuous, and respectful; who are good, capable, trustworthy, and givers of knowledge and wealth—these should be taught according to the Dharma.
He should carry a staff, a deerskin, and a sacred thread, as well as a girdle.
He should go about for alms among blameless Brahmins for the sake of his own subsistence.
The practice of begging for alms by Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas is characterized respectively by the words "bhavat" (lady), placed at the beginning, middle, and end [of the request].
Having performed the fire-rituals, he should eat with speech restrained, by the permission of his teacher,
after performing the *āpośāna* rite, honoring the food and not disparaging it.
Remaining in the stage of studentship (*brahmacarya*), one should not eat food from a single source except in times of distress.
A Brāhmaṇa may, at his will, eat at a *śrāddha* feast, provided he does not violate his vow.

One should avoid honey, meat, collyrium, food-leavings, fermented acids, women, and the harming of living beings; as well as gazing at the sun, vulgar speech, slander, and so forth. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.33)
He is a *guru* who, having performed the rites, imparts the Veda to him; he who, having initiated him, gives him the Veda is designated an *ācārya*.

The teacher who imparts even a single portion [of knowledge] is called an *upādhyāya*; the one who performs the sacrifice is called an *ṛtvij*. These are to be honored according to their precedence; yet among them all, the mother is the most venerable.
For each Veda, the period of studentship (brahmacarya) shall be twelve years or five;
some say it should last until the Veda has been mastered, while others say it ends at the sixteenth year, when the hair is shorn.
Up to the sixteenth, the twenty-second, and the twenty-fourth year, respectively,
is the latest time for the initiation ceremony for those of the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya castes.
From this point forward, these fall [from their caste], excluded from all religious duties;
they are *vrātyas* who have fallen away from the *Sāvitrī*, except through the *Vrātyastoma* sacrifice.
Since Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas are born once from their mother and a second time from the tying of the girdle of Muñja grass, they are therefore remembered as "twice-born."
For the twice-born, the Veda alone is the supreme means for attaining the highest good through sacrifices, austerities, and indeed all auspicious actions.
That twice-born man who studies the Rigveda verses every day satisfies the gods with honey and milk, and the ancestors with honey and clarified butter.
He who studies the Yajus formulas daily according to his ability satisfies the gods with clarified butter and nectar,
and likewise the ancestors with sacrificial butter and honey.
He who recites [this] daily shall satisfy the gods with Soma and clarified butter;
and by means of the Sāman chants, he shall bring satisfaction to the ancestors with honey and ghee.
Reciting the Atharvāṅgirasaḥ, he should satisfy the gods with fat;
and the twice-born man should daily satisfy the ancestors with honey and clarified butter according to his ability.
He who studies daily, according to his ability, the dialogues, the Purāṇas, the Nārāśaṃsīs, the Gāthās, the Itihāsas, and the sciences; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.45.
He provides satisfaction for the dwellers of heaven with meat, milk, rice, and honey;
and he should likewise provide for the ancestors with honey and clarified butter.
When they are satisfied, they satisfy him with auspicious fruits that fulfill all desires; and whatever sacrifice he studies, he shall obtain the fruit of each one of them.

A twice-born man who is constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Veda (svādhyāya) here in this world obtains three times the fruit of gifting the earth filled with wealth, as well as the fruit of supreme austerity.
But a lifelong student (naiṣṭhika) shall dwell in the presence of his teacher; in the absence of the teacher, in the teacher's son, in his wife, or even in the sacred fire.
By this rule, one who has conquered his senses, casting off the body, attains the world of Brahman and is not born again in this world.
[3. Section on Marriage]
Having given a gift to the teacher, or with his permission, he may perform the ceremonial bath;
or having brought the Veda, or the vows, or both to completion.
Having remained steadfast in his vow of celibacy, he should marry a woman who possesses auspicious marks—
one who has not belonged to another before, who is pleasing to him, who is not a sapinda relative, and who is younger than himself.
One who is free from disease, has brothers, and is not born of the same *ārṣa* lineage or *gotra*;
likewise, she who is beyond the fifth on the mother’s side and the seventh on the father’s side;
and she who comes from a great family of *śrotriyas* renowned for ten generations.
Nor from one who, though prosperous, is afflicted by the defect of a contagious disease.

(Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.54c) A bridegroom of the same caste (*savarṇa*) who possesses these very qualities, is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), has been carefully examined for virility, is young, wise, and beloved by the people, is the best. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.55)
As for that which is said— that the taking of a Śūdra woman as a wife by the twice-born—
is not my opinion, because in that case he himself is born [from her].

Three wives are prescribed for the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya respectively, according to the order of the castes; likewise, one wife is for the man born as a Śūdra. Among these, his own [wife] is the one belonging to his own caste.
The Brāhma marriage is that in which [the bride] is given after being invited and having been adorned according to one's ability;
the son born of her purifies twenty-one generations on both sides.
The *daiva* [form] consists of giving [the bride] to the officiating priest at a sacrifice; the *ārṣa*, however, consists of taking two cows.
The son born of the first [form] purifies fourteen [generations], and the one born of the latter [form] purifies six.
Having said this, "May she who is given to a suitor practice dharma together with him," that body, born of her, shall purify six ancestors on each side along with herself.
The Āsura [form] arises from the taking of wealth; the Gāndharva, from mutual agreement;
the Rākṣasa, from abduction by force; and the Paiśāca, from the deception of the maiden.
In marriages with women of the same caste, the hand is to be taken; a Kṣatriya bride should take hold of an arrow, and a Vaiśya bride should take up a goad when marrying one of a higher birth.
The father, the grandfather, the brother, a sapinda relative, and likewise the mother;
in the absence of each preceding one, each subsequent person is the giver of the maiden, provided they are of sound mind.

If he does not give her away, he incurs the guilt of killing an embryo at every menstrual period. However, in the absence of givers, a maiden may choose a husband for herself from among those who are suitable.

A maiden is given only once; he who carries her off [after she has been given] shall be subject to the punishment for theft. Even if she has already been given, he may take her back from the previous giver if a more excellent suitor arrives.
One who gives a gift without disclosing its defect shall be punished with the highest fine;
but one who abandons a faultless gift, or falsely accuses it of being defective, shall be fined one hundred [paṇas].
One who has not been deflowered and one who has been deflowered are both called *punarbhū* if she undergoes the sacramental rite again;
likewise, a *svairiṇī* is she who, having abandoned her husband, out of desire resorts to a man of her own caste.

A brother-in-law, with the permission of the husband's elder, or a sapinda or a sagotra, being anointed with clarified butter, may approach a childless woman during her fertile period with the desire for a son.
He may go [to his mother] until the birth of the child; otherwise, he would become an outcast. A son born according to this rule shall be the "soil-born" (kṣetraja) son of that man.
One should cause an unfaithful wife to dwell deprived of her authority, defiled, subsisting on mere morsels of food, humiliated, and sleeping on the ground.
Soma gave them purity, and the Gandharva gave them beautiful speech; Pāvaka [Fire] gave them fitness for all sacrificial rites, for women are indeed pure.
Purification is prescribed for adultery during the fertile period;
abandonment is ordained in the case of pregnancy, as well as for the murder of the husband or other such great sins.

A woman who drinks liquor, one who is diseased, a rogue, one who is barren, one who destroys wealth, one who speaks unpleasantly, one who bears only daughters, and likewise one who hates her husband— such a wife may be superseded by taking another.
But a superseded wife (adhivinnā) must be maintained; otherwise, a great sin would ensue.
Where there is mutual harmony between husband and wife, there the three goals of life (trivarga) flourish.
Whether her husband is dead or living, she who does not approach another man attains fame in this world and rejoices with him in the hereafter.

If he abandons a wife who obeys his commands, is skillful, bears him heroic sons, and speaks kindly, he should be made to pay a third part of his estate; if he possesses no property, he must provide maintenance for her.
Wives must carry out their husband's command; this is the highest duty of a woman.
For one defiled by a mortal sin (mahāpātaka) must indeed be awaited until purification.
Since the infinity of worlds and the attainment of heaven are achieved through sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons,
therefore women should be enjoyed and well protected.

Women have sixteen nights during their fertile season; among these, he should approach her on the even nights. He should remain as one practicing celibacy (*brahmacārī*) and avoid the sacred festival days (*parvan*) as well as the first four nights.
Proceeding in this manner, he should avoid a woman who is emaciated, as well as the constellations Maghā and Mūla;
when the moon is in its full strength, a man shall procreate a single, auspiciously marked son.
Or he may act according to his desire, remembering the boon granted to women;
yet he should remain devoted to his own wife, for women are declared to be worthy of protection.
Women are to be honored by their husbands, brothers, fathers, paternal kinsmen,
mothers-in-law, fathers-in-law, brothers-in-law, and relatives with ornaments, clothing, and food.
Keeping the household utensils well-ordered, being skillful, cheerful, and averse to wasteful expenditure,
she should perform the salutation of the feet of her parents-in-law, being entirely devoted to her husband.
A woman whose husband is away on a journey should abandon play, bodily adornment, attendance at social gatherings and festivals, laughter, and visiting the houses of others.
The father shall protect the maiden; her husband, when she is married; and her sons in old age. In their absence, her paternal kinsmen shall protect her; a woman is never independent.
A woman should not be deprived [of her property] by her father, mother, son, brother, mother-in-law, father-in-law, or maternal uncles;
she may not be so deprived except by her husband, otherwise she would become censurable.
Devoted to the pleasure and welfare of her husband, conducting herself according to her own proper discipline, and having conquered her senses,
she attains fame in this world and the highest state after death.
If another wife of the same caste exists, one should not have religious duties performed by her;
among wives of the same caste who are eligible for religious rites, none other may be employed in the prescribed duty except the eldest.

Having cremated his virtuous wife with the *agnihotra* fire, the husband should, without delay, take another wife and the sacred fires according to the prescribed rule. [Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.89] (Chapter 4:
Distinction of Classes and Castes)
From men of the same caste, upon women of the same caste, are born those of the same lineage;
through blameless marriages, sons are produced who increase the progeny.
From a Brāhmaṇa father and a Kṣatriya mother is born the Mūrdhāvasikta; from the same father and a Vaiśya woman, the Ambaṣṭha; and from a Śūdra woman, the Niṣāda or the Pāraśava.

From a Vaiśya father and a Kṣatriya mother, the Māhiṣya and the Ugra are declared to be the two sons; from a Vaiśya father and a Śūdra mother, the Karaṇa is born. This is the rule recorded for wives who have been duly married.
From a Kṣatriya on a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Sūta; likewise, from a Vaiśya, a Vaidehaka;
but from a Śūdra on a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Caṇḍāla, who is excluded from all religious duties.
From a Vaiśya father and a Kṣatriya mother, a Māgadha is born; from a Śūdra father, a Kṣattṛ is born.
Furthermore, from a Śūdra father and a Vaiśya mother, a Vaiśya woman indeed gives birth to an Āyogava son.
From a Māhiṣya father and a Karaṇī mother, a Rathakāra is born;
these, however, are to be known as those born in the inverse and natural orders of castes.
The elevation of caste should be understood to occur in the seventh or even the fifth generation;
upon the reversal of occupations, there is equality, and as before, the lower and higher status are determined accordingly. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.96) [5.
The Section on the Duties of the Householder] (p. 33)
A householder should perform every day the *smārta* rites in the marriage fire,
or those performed at the time of inheritance, or the *śrauta* rites in the *vaitānika* fires.
Having attended to the needs of the body and performed the prescribed rites of purification,
the twice-born man should perform the morning twilight devotion (*prātaḥ-saṃdhyā*), preceded by the cleansing of the teeth.
Having offered oblations into the fires dedicated to Sūrya, he should, with a concentrated mind, mutter the mantras;
and he should master the meanings of the Vedas as well as various treatises.
And he should approach a lord for the sake of accomplishing his goals regarding acquisition and preservation;
having bathed, he should likewise offer libations to and worship the gods and the ancestors.

For the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice of recitation (japa-yajña), he should, according to his ability, recite the Vedas, the Atharvaveda, the Purāṇas along with the Itihāsas, and spiritual knowledge (vidyā).
The offering of the *bali*, the *svadhā* oblation, the fire-sacrifice (*homa*), the private recitation of scripture (*svādhyāya*), and the hospitable reception of guests—
these are the great sacrifices to the beings, the ancestors, the gods, Brahman, and human beings.
From the food remaining after the oblation has been offered to the gods, one should present the *bhūtabali*;
one should also place food on the ground for dogs, *caṇḍālas*, and crows.
Food should be given daily to the ancestors and to human beings, as well as water;
one should constantly perform the private recitation of the Veda, and one should not cook food for oneself alone.
Having fed the children, the women living in their fathers' houses, the elderly, pregnant women, the sick,
and young girls, as well as guests and dependents, the husband and wife should eat what remains.
A twice-born man, while eating, should ensure that his food is neither naked nor immortal by performing the *āpośana* rite both before and after.
To the various social classes, one should give according to one's ability and in due order by virtue of their status as guests;
a guest must not be turned away in the evening, even if offered only words, a place to lie down, grass, and water.
Having honored the mendicant, alms should be given to him who observes his vows;
and one should feed friends, relatives, and kinsmen when they arrive at the proper time.
One should provide a large bull or a large goat to a learned Brahmin (śrotriya), along with hospitable treatment,
a seat, delicious food, and pleasant speech.
But every year, the Snātaka, the teacher, the king, a dear friend, one for whom one is performing a marriage, and likewise the officiating priests at a sacrifice, are worthy of the Arghya offering.
A traveler who has reached his destination and a *śrotriya* who has mastered the Vedas are to be known as guests; these two are to be honored by a householder desiring the world of Brahman.
One should not have a craving for the food cooked by others, except when invited by those who are blameless; one should also avoid fickleness of speech, hands, and feet, as well as overeating.
He should follow the guest who is a learned Vedic scholar until he is satisfied and has departed from the boundary;
for the remainder of the day, he should sit together with refined persons, beloved friends, and kinsmen.
Having performed the evening twilight worship, having offered oblations into those fires,
and having eaten with his dependents until he is no longer hungry, he should then go to sleep.
Having risen during the *muhūrta* sacred to Brahmā, he should reflect upon his own welfare;
he should not neglect virtue (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), and pleasure (*kāma*) at their proper times, according to his ability.
They are to be honored in order according to learning, ritual action, age, kinship, and wealth;
even a Śūdra, if he possesses these in abundance, deserves honor in his old age.

The way must be yielded to the elderly, those carrying burdens, kings, bath-graduates, women, the sick, bridegrooms, and those in vehicles; among these, the king is to be honored by them, and the bath-graduate is to be honored by the king.
Sacrificing, studying, and giving are the duties of both the Vaiśya and the Kṣatriya;
however, for the Brāhmaṇa, there are additionally the receiving of gifts, as well as officiating at sacrifices and teaching.
The primary duty of a Kṣatriya is the protection of the subjects;
for a Vaiśya, moneylending, agriculture, trade, and cattle-rearing are prescribed.
The duty of a Śūdra is service to the twice-born; if he cannot subsist by that, he may become a merchant, or he may live by various crafts while acting for the benefit of the twice-born.
Delighting in his wife, pure, supporting his dependents, and devoted to the performance of ancestral rites,
he should not neglect the five sacrifices by means of the mantra of salutation.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, purity, and restraint of the senses;
generosity, self-control, compassion, and forbearance—these are the means for accomplishing the dharma for all.
One should likewise adopt a conduct that is consistent with one's age, intelligence, wealth, speech, dress, learning, lineage, and actions— conduct that is straightforward and free from deceit.
A twice-born man who possesses more than a three-year supply of food may indeed drink the Soma;
he whose food lasts for one year may perform the rites preliminary to the Soma sacrifice.
Every year, the Soma sacrifice, the animal sacrifice, and likewise the Pratyāyanīya;
the Āgrayaṇeṣṭi and the Cāturmāsya sacrifices must indeed be performed.
In the absence of these [materials], a twice-born man should perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice;
he should not perform a deficient rite when the necessary substances are available, for it yields no fruit.
By performing a sacrifice using wealth begged from a Śūdra, one is born as a Cāṇḍāla;
if one does not give away what was obtained for the sake of a sacrifice, one becomes a vulture or even a crow.
Or he may possess grain sufficient for a granary or a jar; or he may have enough for three days, or even not enough for the morrow.
Or he may live by gleaning ears of corn and picking up single grains; among these, each succeeding mode is superior to the preceding one.
One should not seek wealth that conflicts with one's Vedic study from whatever source it may come;
nor should one always indulge in forbidden pursuits, but remain contented.
If, while living with them, he should desire wealth due to hunger, he may seek it from a king, a resident pupil, or his own patron;
however, he should avoid those who are hypocritical, those who argue for the sake of gain, heretics, and those who live like herons.
Wearing white garments, with his hair, beard, and nails clipped short, and being pure,
he should not eat while looking at his wife, nor while wearing only a single garment, nor while standing.
One should not fall into doubt, nor should one speak unpleasantly without cause;
one should neither speak what is harmful nor what is untrue, nor should one be a thief, nor a usurer.
Wearing a girdle of muñja grass, the sacred thread, carrying a bamboo staff and a water-pot,
he should circumambulate clockwise the gods, clay, cows, Brahmins, and trees.
But one should not urinate in a river, in shade, on a path, in a cow-pen, in water, or on ashes;
nor should one face the fire, the sun, a cow, the moon, the two twilights, water, a woman, or a twice-born man.
One should not look at the sun, nor at a naked woman, nor at one engaged in sexual intercourse;
nor at urine or excrement, nor at impure things, nor at the stars of Rāhu.
One should recite the entire mantra thus: "This is my thunderbolt.
When it rains, one should go about uncovered; nor should one sleep with the head toward the west.
One should not cast spittle, blood, feces, urine, or semen into water;
one should not warm one's feet over a fire, nor should one step over it.
One should not drink water with joined palms, nor should one wake a sleeping person.
One should not play with dice, nor should one lie down with those who destroy dharma or with those who are diseased.
One should avoid forbidden actions, such as crossing a river by blowing through the smoke of a funeral pyre, and one should not sit upon hair, ashes, chaff, embers, or potsherds.
One should not report a cow suckling her calf, nor should one ever enter through any opening other than the door;
one should not accept gifts from a greedy king who acts in contravention of the scriptures.
In receiving gifts, the outcaste, the oil-presser, the liquor-seller, the prostitute,
and the king are each ten times more corrupt than the one preceding them, respectively.
The commencement of the study of the Vedas (upākarma) shall take place on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, or under the asterism Śravaṇa,
or under the asterism Hasta when the medicinal herbs have appeared, or on the fifth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa.
On the Rohiṇī day of the month of Pauṣa, or likewise on the Aṣṭakā day,
one should perform the formal ritual of the dismissal of the Vedas (chandasām utsarga) outside at the edge of the water.
There is a suspension of study for three days when pupils, officiating priests, teachers, or kinsmen have died;
likewise upon the commencement (upākarmaṇi) and the conclusion (utsarge) of the Vedic term, and when a master of one's own Vedic branch has passed away.
[In the case of a learned scholar of one's own Vedic school: Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.145:
Upon the thundering of clouds at twilight, a thunderclap, an earthquake, or the falling of a meteor;
and having completed the study of the Veda, or having studied the *Āraṇyaka*, one should remain for a day and a night.

On the fifteenth day, the fourteenth day, the eighth day, during an eclipse, at the junctions of the seasons, or after eating at a funeral feast (śrāddha) or accepting a gift from such a feast; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.146.
If [the sacrificial fire] is touched by a domestic animal, a frog, a mongoose, a dog, a snake, a cat, or a mouse, one must fast for a day and a night;
the same applies when lightning strikes or when there is an earthquake.
When there is the sound of a dog, a jackal, a donkey, an owl, a *sāman* chant, an arrow, or one who is distressed;
or when one is near impure matter, a corpse, a *śūdra*, an outcaste (*antya*), a cremation ground, or a fallen person.

In an impure place, when one is personally impure, during the simultaneous occurrence of lightning and thunder, after eating while the hands are still wet, in the midst of water, at midnight, or during a violent wind; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.149.

During a shower of dust, when the quarters of the sky are ablaze, during the twilight hours, in mist, or when there is fear; while running, when there is a foul odor, or when a learned man has arrived at one's house—[in these cases, one may eat even without washing].
When riding on a donkey, a camel, a carriage, an elephant, a horse, or a boat; when climbing a tree, a barren spot, or a mountain—these they know as the thirty-seven temporary interruptions of study.
One should not step upon the shadow of a deity, an officiating priest, a bath-graduate, a teacher, or a king, nor that of another's wife;
nor should one step upon blood, feces, urine, spittle, ointments for the body, and the like.
The Brahmin, the snake, and the Kṣatriya—these three souls are never to be despised.
Until death one should desire prosperity; one should not touch anyone on their vital spot.
One should cast away remnants of food, feces, urine, and water from a distance;
one should always practice the conduct of right behavior as fully prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti.
One who is impure from eating should not touch a cow, a Brāhmaṇa, fire, or food with his feet;
he should neither revile nor strike them, though he may strike his son or pupil [for correction].
One should diligently practice dharma through deed, mind, and speech; however, one should not practice even that which is technically dharma if it leads away from heaven or is despised by the world.
With mother, father, guests, brothers, sisters, relatives, maternal uncles;
and with the elderly, children, the sick, teachers, physicians, dependents, and kinsmen.
By avoiding disputes with officiating priests, family chaplains, children, wives, slaves, and blood relatives, a householder shall conquer all the worlds.
One should not bathe in the waters of others without first taking up five lumps of earth;
however, one may bathe in rivers, natural reservoirs of the gods, lakes, and springs.
One should avoid the beds, seats, gardens, houses, and vehicles of others; one should not eat the food of one who maintains no sacred fire, except in times of distress.
Of the miserly, the bound, and thieves; of eunuchs, actors, and those who enter the stage;
of flute-players, the accused, usurers, courtesans, and those initiated for a group sacrifice.
[One should not eat the food] of physicians, the sick, the angry, unchaste women, the intoxicated, and those who bear enmity;
nor [the food] of the cruel, the fierce, the outcastes (patita), the vrātyas, the hypocritical, and those who eat the leavings of others.
[The food] of a woman without a male relative, of a goldsmith, of a woman conquered by her husband, of one who sacrifices for an entire village,
of a seller of weapons, of a blacksmith, of a weaver, and of one who lives by dogs [is impure].
[The impurity lasts for ten days] for those who kill a cruel man, a king, a washerman, an ungrateful person, or one who lives by slaughter;
and for a clothes-washer, a liquor-seller, and those who live in the house of a paramour.
The food of the slanderer and the liar, as well as that of the professional storyteller and the bard, and likewise that of the seller of Soma— of these, one must not eat.

Among Śūdras, the food of a slave, a cowherd, a family friend, a plowshare-mate, and a barber may be eaten; as may the food of one who offers himself [as a servant]. [Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.166] (Section 7:
On Edible and Non-edible Food)

Meat that has not been honored, meat not intended for sacrifice, meat containing hair or insects, that which is sour, stale, or leftover, that which has been touched by a dog, or that which has been looked upon by an outcast; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.167.
One should avoid food touched by a menstruating woman, food announced [in advance], and food served in turns;
as well as food smelled by a cow, the leavings of birds, and that which has been intentionally touched with the foot.
Food that has stood overnight may be eaten if it is mixed with oil or fat and has been kept for a long time;
likewise, preparations of wheat, barley, and cow's milk may be eaten even if they are not mixed with oil or fat.
One should avoid the milk of a cow that is in heat, one whose calf has not yet passed ten days,
a camel, any single-hoofed animal, a female animal, a wild animal, and a sheep.
One should avoid sacrificial oblations intended for the deities, the marking-nut (*śigru*), red exudations from incisions,
meat that has not been consecrated with ritual formulas, things produced from filth, and mushrooms.
Flesh-eating birds, the dātyūha, the parrot, pecking birds, the ṭiṭṭibha, the sārasa crane, single-hoofed animals, swans, and all those dwelling in villages; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.172.
The koyaṣṭi, the plava, the cakrāhva, the balākā, the baka, and the viṣkira birds;
and kṛsara, saṃyāva, pāyasa, apūpa, and śaṣkulī prepared for no sacred purpose.
The kalaviṅka, the crow, the osprey, the rajjudālaka, web-footed birds, the khanjarīṭa, and unknown species of animals and birds.
Having intentionally eaten blue jays, red-footed birds, the flesh of a dog, dried meat, or fish, one should dwell for three days observing a fast.
Having eaten onions, village pigs, mushrooms, village cocks,
garlic, and leeks, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Among five-toed animals, the porcupine, the monitor lizard, the tortoise, the pangolin, and the hare are edible;
likewise, among fish, the siṃhatuṇḍaka and the rohita are edible.
Likewise, the *pāṭhīna*, the *rājīva*, and the *saśalka* fish may be eaten by the twice-born. Therefore, listen to the rule regarding the eating and the avoidance of meat.
In a life-threatening situation, at a Śrāddha ceremony, when meat has been consecrated with water, or when requested by a twice-born,
one who eats meat after having worshipped the gods and the ancestors incurs no fault.
That man of evil conduct who kills animals contrary to the prescribed rule shall dwell in a terrible hell for as many days as there are hairs on the bodies of those animals.
A Brahmin who abstains from meat, even while living at home, obtains all his desires as well as the fruit of the horse sacrifice; he becomes a sage. [Chapter 8:
On the Purification of Substances]
Of gold, silver, and lotuses; of vessels with upward openings, water-vessels, and stones; of vegetables, ropes, roots, fruits, garments, split bamboo, and skins.
The purification of drinking vessels and cups is prescribed to be by means of water;
however, the *caru* pot, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, and vessels containing oily substances are purified with hot water.

The sprinkling of purification (prokṣaṇa) is prescribed for the wooden sword (sphya), the winnowing basket (śūrpa), the skin (ajina), and grains; for the pestle (musala), the mortar (ulūkhala), and the cart (anaḥ); and for many grains and garments when they are piled together.

The cleaning of objects made of wood, horn, or bone is by means of cow-hair; that of vessels produced from fruit is by means of cow-hair; and the cleaning of sacrificial vessels during a ritual act is with the hand.
Woolen cloth (*āvika*) and silk (*kauśika*) are purified by saline earth, water, and cow urine;
linen cloth (*aṃśupaṭṭa*) by *śrīphala* fruits, and likewise woolen blanket (*kutapa*) by *ariṣṭa* fruits.
Silk is purified by white mustard seeds, and earthenware by re-firing;
the hand of an artisan, food obtained as alms, and the mouth of a woman are likewise pure.
The purification of the ground is achieved by sweeping, by burning, by the passage of time, and likewise by the treading of cows;
furthermore, a house is purified by sprinkling, by scraping, by smearing, and by sweeping and smearing.
When food has been smelled by a cow, or likewise defiled by hair, flies, or insects,
water, ashes, or even earth should be cast into it for the sake of purification.
Tin, lead, and copper are purified by alkaline substances, acids, water, and cow-urine;
bell-metal and iron are purified by ashes and water; and for liquids, purification is by means of straining.
That which is smeared with impure substances is purified by earth and water through the removal of odor and the like;
that which is praised by word, washed with water, and that which is unknown are always pure.
Water on the ground that is naturally pure and sufficient to satisfy a cow is pure;
likewise is meat that has been brought down by dogs, Caṇḍālas, carnivorous beasts, and the like.
A ray of light, fire, dust, shadow, a cow, a horse, the earth, and the wind;
droplets and flies are pure when touched; and a calf is pure when suckling.
The mouths of goats and horses are pure, but those of cows and humans are not;
likewise, roads are purified by the rays of the moon and sun and by the wind.

Drops from the mouth are pure, as are drops from the water used for sipping; likewise, a beard and hair inside the mouth are pure, and one becomes pure after removing what is stuck between the teeth. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.195)
Having bathed, drunk, sneezed, slept, eaten, or walked upon a road,
and after putting on a different garment, one who has already sipped water should sip water again.
Roads, mud, and water touched by outcastes, dogs,
or crows are purified by the wind alone, as are structures built with baked bricks.
Having performed austerities, Brahmā created the Brāhmaṇas for the protection of the Vedas,
for the satisfaction of the ancestors and the gods, and for the preservation of Dharma.
Brahmins who are devoted to Vedic learning and study are the source of all;
among them, those devoted to ritual action are superior, and even more excellent than they are those who possess the highest knowledge of the inner self.
Neither by learning alone nor even by austerity is one a worthy recipient;
rather, that person in whom both of these, as well as good conduct, reside is proclaimed to be a worthy recipient.
Cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, and so forth should be given with honor to a worthy recipient;
a wise man who desires his own welfare should not give anything at all to an unworthy recipient.
A gift must not be accepted by one who is deficient in learning and austerity;
for by accepting it, he leads both the giver and himself downward.
One should give daily to a worthy recipient, especially on specific occasions;
even when requested, one should give according to one's ability, purified by faith.
A milch cow with golden horns and silver hooves, well-tempered, provided with a cloth, accompanied by a bronze vessel, and given along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), should be bestowed.
The giver of this [cow] attains heaven for as many years as there are hairs on her body;
if she is tawny (*kapilā*), she delivers his lineage even further, up to the seventh generation.
By giving a cow with her calf that has two faces, the giver attains heaven for as many ages as there are hairs on its body, according to the previously mentioned rite.
As long as both the feet and the face of the calf are visible within the womb,
for that long the cow should be known as the Earth, as long as she does not release the fetus.
By giving a cow, whether it be a milch-cow or even one that is not, in whatever manner possible—
provided it is healthy and free from affliction— the donor is glorified in heaven.
Massaging those who are weary, attending to the sick, worshipping the gods,
washing the feet of the twice-born, and clearing away their remnants are equal to the gift of a cow.
By giving land, lamps, food, clothing, water, sesame seeds, clarified butter, shelter, a house, gold, and draft animals, one is glorified in heaven.
By giving a house, grain, protection from fear, sandals, an umbrella, garlands, ointments, a vehicle, a tree, a beloved object, or a bed, one becomes exceedingly happy.
Since Brahman, which consists of all dharmas, is superior to all gifts,
one who gives it attains the imperishable world of Brahman.
Even though he is capable of accepting gifts, he who does not accept them attains those abundant worlds which belong to those whose nature is to give.
Kuśa grass, vegetables, milk, fish, perfumes, flowers,
curd, land, meat, a bed, a seat, parched grain, and water— these should not be refused.
Food brought unsolicited may be accepted even from one who has committed evil deeds,
except in the case of unchaste women, eunuchs, outcasts, and enemies.
For the sake of honoring gods and guests, for the sake of his teacher and dependents, or indeed for his own subsistence, he may accept gifts from anyone at all. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.216)
The new moon day, the Aṣṭakās, an occasion of prosperity, the dark fortnight, the two solstices,
the availability of materials, the presence of worthy Brahmins, the equinox, and the sun’s passage into a new zodiacal sign.
Vyatīpāta, Gajacchāyā, the eclipses of the moon and the sun,
and a personal inclination toward performing a Śrāddha— these are proclaimed as the proper times for a Śrāddha.
One who is foremost among all the Vedas, a śrotriya, a knower of Brahman, and young;
one who knows the meaning of the Veda, a master of the Jyeṣṭhasāman, a Tri-madhu, and a Tri-suparṇaka.
The sister’s son, the officiating priest, the son-in-law, the person for whom one sacrifices, the father-in-law, the maternal uncle;
the one who has performed the Triṇāciketa rite, the daughter’s son, the pupil, the relative by marriage, and the kinsman.

Those who are devoted to ritual action, those devoted to austerity, those who maintain the five sacred fires, celibate students, and those who are devoted to their fathers and mothers— these are the Brāhmaṇas who constitute the perfection of the Śrāddha.

One who is diseased, one with missing or extra limbs, one who is one-eyed, one born of a remarried woman, one who has broken his vow of chastity, the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*, one with deformed nails, and one with black teeth; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.222.

A teacher for hire, a eunuch, a defiler of virgins, one accused of a heinous crime, a betrayer of friends, a slanderer, a seller of Soma, and one who marries before his elder brother; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.223.

One who abandons mother, father, or guru; one who eats the food of a *kuṇḍa*; the son of a *vṛṣala* (low-caste man); the husband of a woman previously married to another; a thief; and those whose actions are corrupt—these are censured.
On the day before [the ceremony], the self-possessed and pure host should invite the Brāhmaṇas;
they too must remain restrained in their actions of mind, speech, and body.
In the afternoon, having honored those who have arrived with a welcome, he—
holding purifying grass in his hand and after they have sipped water— should cause them to sit upon their seats.
One should invite an even number of Brahmins for the rite to the gods according to one's ability, and likewise an odd number for the rite to the ancestors;
this should be done in a purified place that is well-spread with grass and slopes toward the south.
Two for the gods facing east, three for the ancestors facing north, or even one for each;
the same applies to the maternal grandfathers, or the Vaiśvadeva rite may be performed as a single common offering (tantra).
Having provided water for washing the hands and also *kuśa* grass for seats, he should, being authorized, invoke [the ancestors] with the verse beginning "O Viśvedevas... (RV X.15.3).
Then, having scattered barley grains into a vessel provided with purifiers (*pavitra*),
and having poured water with the verse *śaṃ no devīr*, he likewise pours barley grains with the formula *yavo 'si*.
With the mantra "yā divyā," he should pour the *arghya* water into their hands;
having offered water, fragrance, garlands, incense, and lamps,
as well as a gift of clothing and water for the purpose of washing the hands.
Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder, he should perform the circumambulation of the ancestors in a counter-clockwise direction.
Having given double-folded *kuśa* grass blades while reciting the verse "Oṣaṇtas tvā," and having invoked the ancestors, he should, with their permission, mutter the verse "Āyantu naḥ" thereafter.

Having scattered sesame seeds all around with the words "apahatāḥ" (the demons are struck down), one should perform the rites for which barley is intended using sesame seeds; one should offer the guest-water (*arghya*) and so forth as before.
Having offered the *arghya* water and having placed their remnants in a vessel according to the rule,
he turns the vessel face down with the mantra "Thou art the seat for the ancestors."

When he intends to offer [the oblation] in the fire, he takes up food soaked in clarified butter and asks, "Shall I sacrifice? Having been authorized with the reply, "Do so," he sacrifices in the fire as in the Pitṛyajña.
Having composed his mind, he should offer the remnants of the oblation into vessels made of whatever materials are available,
and especially into those made of silver.
Having given the food, one should consecrate the vessel with the mantra, "The earth is the vessel" (Yājñavalkya 1.238a).
Having performed this, one should place the thumb of the twice-born guest into the food with the mantra, "Viṣṇu pervaded this" (Yājñavalkya 1.238c).
Having recited the Gāyatrī with the vyāhṛtis and the three verses beginning with "madhu vātā," they should eat while remaining silent, speaking only as necessary for their comfort.
One should give food that is desirable and fit for oblation, free from anger and without haste;
and one should recite purifying mantras as well as the previously mentioned prayers until satiety.
Having taken food [and asked], "Are you satisfied? and having obtained permission regarding the remainder, one should scatter that food on the ground and offer water once for each [guest].
Having taken all the food together with sesame seeds, facing the south,
he should offer the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) near the remnants of the meal, just as in the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*).
In the same manner, one should likewise offer water for sipping to the maternal grandfathers;
thereafter, one should cause the benediction "svasti" to be recited and also offer the water for inexhaustibility (*akṣayyodaka*).
Having given the sacrificial fee according to his ability, he should utter the word *svadhā*.
Being authorized with the words "Let it be spoken," he should say to the invited ancestors, "Let the *svadhā* be pronounced."
When they have said, "Let it be; Svadhā," one should pour water on the ground.
Then, [the performer] should say, "May the Viśvedevas be pleased," and when this has been spoken by the Brahmins, he should mutter this [mantra].
"May our givers increase, as well as the Vedas and our progeny;
may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give."
Having spoken these kind words and having prostrated,
he should dismiss [the guests] with the words "vāje vāje," while being pleased, performing the dismissal beginning with the ancestors.
But that vessel for the ancestors into which the previous remnants had first been poured, one should turn upside down and then dismiss the Brahmins.
Having circumambulated [the place] clockwise, he should eat what was served to the ancestors;
on that night, however, he should remain a *brahmacārī* together with the Brahmins.

Thus, having performed the circumambulation from left to right, one should sacrifice to the Nāndīmukha ancestors on the occasion of prosperity; the offerings consist of balls of food mixed with curd and jujube fruits, and the rites are performed with barley.

The *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is devoid of offerings to the gods; it has a single *arghya* offering and a single *pavitraka*; indeed, it is performed without the *āvāhana* and *agnaukaraṇa* rites, and with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*).
At the dismissal of the Brahmins, in place of the word "akṣayya," he should say, "May [the ancestors] be satisfied" (*upatiṣṭhatām*);
they should then say, "We are satisfied" (*abhiratāḥ sma*).
One should prepare four vessels containing fragrant water and sesame seeds;
for the purpose of the *arghya* offering, one should pour the vessel of the deceased (*preta*) into the vessels of the ancestors (*pitṛ*).
With the two verses beginning "Those who are equal," he should perform the remainder as previously described.
This is the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite; for a woman also, it is performed as a single-destination offering (eka-uddiṣṭa).
If for anyone the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite has occurred before the completion of one year,
one should provide food along with a water-pot to a twice-born man for the duration of that year.
On the anniversary of the day of death, the rite should be performed every month for a year;
likewise, it should be performed annually, with the first one being on the eleventh day.
One should give the funeral balls (*piṇḍas*) to cows, goats, or Brahmins, or else cast them into fire or water.
While Brahmins are present, one should not wipe away the remnants of the twice-born's meal.
By means of sacrificial food (haviṣya-anna) one indeed [attains the goal] for a month, but by milk-rice (pāyasa) for a year;
likewise by the meat of fish, deer, kuraṅga, birds, goat, and spotted deer.
The ancestors, when offered here the meats of the black antelope, the Ruru deer, the boar, and the hare, respectively,
remain satisfied for an increasing number of months.
The meat of the rhinoceros, large-scaled fish, honey, or the food of ascetics;
the meat of the red goat, large vegetables, and the flesh of the Vārdhrīṇasa crane.
Whatever one who stays at Gayā gives, all that becomes infinite;
likewise on the thirteenth day of the rainy season, and especially under the Maghā asterism.
A maiden, those who recognize maidens, cattle, and even virtuous sons;
gambling, agriculture, trade, as well as animals with cloven and uncloven hooves.
The giver of a Śrāddha always obtains sons endowed with Vedic luster, gold and silver along with base metals, preeminence among kinsmen, and all desires.
On the days beginning with the first lunar day, excluding the fourteenth,
that which is offered there is for those who have been slain by weapons.
For one obtains heaven, offspring, vigor, heroism, a field, strength, as well as a preeminent son, good fortune, prosperity, leadership, and auspiciousness. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.265)
He also attains the status of one whose wheel of sovereignty rolls unimpeded, as well as success in trade and other such pursuits,
freedom from disease, renown, the absence of sorrow, and the supreme goal.
He who duly bestows wealth, the Vedas, medical success, base metals, cattle, goats and sheep, horses, and long life upon one performing a Śrāddha, [attains great merit].
One who possesses faith, is full of devotion, and is free from pride and envy, shall obtain these desires by performing [the rites] beginning with Kṛttikā and ending with Bharaṇī.
The Vasus, Rudras, and sons of Aditi are the ancestors who are the deities of the Śrāddha;
when satiated by the Śrāddha, they gratify the ancestors of human beings.
The ancestors, when pleased, bestow upon men longevity, progeny, wealth, knowledge, heaven, liberation, and happiness, as well as sovereignty. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.270)
Vināyaka was appointed by Rudra and likewise by Brahmā for the purpose of creating obstacles to ritual actions and for the lordship over the Gaṇas.
Learn now the symptoms of one who is possessed by him:
in his dreams, he plunges excessively into water and sees shaven-headed men.
He wears saffron-colored garments and mounts carnivorous beasts;
he stands together with outcastes, donkeys, and camels in one place.
Even while walking, he considers himself followed by others;
dejected and with his undertakings fruitless, he desponds without apparent cause.
Afflicted by him, a prince does not obtain the kingdom; a maiden does not find a husband, nor does a woman conceive offspring or a fetus.

A student who eats at the house of his teacher does not attain the status of a teacher nor the title of a learned scholar (śrotriya), nor does he obtain instruction; likewise, a farmer who eats there does not obtain profit from trade, nor does he gain success in agriculture.
On an auspicious day, his ceremonial bath should be performed according to the prescribed rules;
and after he has been anointed with a paste of white mustard seeds mixed with clarified butter.

Likewise, for one whose head is anointed with all medicinal herbs and all fragrant substances and who is seated upon an auspicious throne, the auspicious twice-born ones should be invoked to pronounce blessings.
One should cast into the water earth from a horse stable, an elephant stable, an anthill, a confluence, and a lake,
as well as yellow pigment, fragrant substances, and bdellium.
Having brought water from a lake in four jars of a single color,
one should then place the auspicious seat upon the hide of a red bull.
With that which has a thousand eyes and a hundred streams, purified by the seers, I sprinkle you; may the Pāvamānī verses purify you.
"May King Varuṇa grant you fortune; may Sūrya and Bṛhaspati grant you fortune;
may Indra and Vāyu grant you fortune, and may the seven Ṛṣis grant you fortune."
Whatever misfortune is in your hair, whatever is in your parting, or whatever is in your head;
may the waters always destroy that which is in your forehead, your ears, and your eyes.
Having bathed, he should offer mustard oil with a ladle made of Udumbara wood,
while holding Kuśa grass with his left hand, upon his head.
Mita, Sammita, Śāla, Kaṭaṅkaṭa,
Kūśmāṇḍa, and Rājaputra— with these names, ending with the word "svāhā," [one should offer oblations].

Having spread *kuśa* grass on all sides upon a winnowing basket at a crossroads, he should offer [the oblation] with their names and with *bali*-mantras accompanied by the word "namas," using both husked and unhusked rice grains as well as rice mixed with sesame paste (*palala-odana*).
Likewise, cooked fish and raw fish, as well as meat—this much is the same.
Variegated and fragrant flowers, the three kinds of *surā* liquor, radishes, *pūrikā* cakes, *apūpa* cakes, as well as *uṇḍeraka* cakes and garlands;
Having collected all these— curd, rice, milk-rice, flour mixed with jaggery, and sweetmeats— and having placed them on the ground, he should then place his head there.
Thereafter, one should worship Ambikā, the mother of Vināyaka, having offered a full añjali of water for honor (*arghya*) consisting of *dūrvā* grass, mustard seeds, and flowers:
"Grant me beauty; grant me fame; grant me fortune, O Bhavānī!"
"Give me sons, give me wealth, and grant me all my desires."
Then, wearing white garments and adorned with white garlands and unguents,
he should feed the Brāhmaṇas and also give a pair of garments to his Guru.
Having thus worshipped Vināyaka and the planets according to the prescribed rule,
one obtains the fruit of one's actions and attains unsurpassed prosperity.
By always performing worship of the Sun, as well as the *tilaka* of one’s own lord and that of Mahāgaṇapati, one shall attain success. [12.
The Section on the Pacification of the Planets]
One who desires prosperity, one who desires tranquility, one who desires rain, long life, or nourishment, or likewise one performing malevolent rites, should perform the sacrifice to the planets.
The Sun, the Moon, the Son of the Earth (Mars), the Son of the Moon (Mercury), Bṛhaspati, Śukra, Śanaiścara, Rāhu, and Ketu— these are known as the planets.
The planetary images should be made, respectively, from copper, crystal, red sandalwood, gold, silver, iron, lead,
and bell-metal.
Or they may be drawn by members of their own respective castes on a cloth, or within mandalas using fragrant pigments;
likewise, garments and flowers should be offered according to their respective colors.
Fragrances, offerings, and incense—specifically guggulu—should be presented; and oblations accompanied by mantras must be performed for each respective deity.
The verses "ākṛṣṇena," "imam devāḥ," "agnir mūrdhā divaḥ kakut," and "udbudhyasva" are proclaimed to be used respectively.
"O Bṛhaspati, that which exceeds the noble ones, likewise from the flowing food;
'May the goddesses be auspicious to us,' likewise from the section; 'making this the banner,' likewise."
The *arka*, *palāśa*, *khadira*, *apāmārga*, and *pippala*;
the *udumbara*, *śamī*, *dūrvā*, and *kuśa* grasses are the sacrificial fuels (*samidh*) in their respective order.
For each [deity], however, one hundred and eight or indeed twenty-eight oblations should be offered,
mixed with honey and clarified butter, or with curds or milk.
Jaggery-rice, milk-rice, and sacrificial food made of *ṣaṣṭika* rice with milk;
curd-rice, sacrificial oblation, flour-meal, meat, and variegated dishes.
The wise man should thus provide food to the twice-born according to the sequence of the planets,
according to his capacity or as it may be obtained, having honored them with due ceremony and in accordance with the prescribed rule.
A milch-cow, a conch-shell, likewise a bull, gold, a garment, and a horse in sequence;
a black cow, iron, and a goat—these indeed are recorded as the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās).
And whoever is in distress at any time should honor that person with effort;
for a boon was granted to them by Brahmā: "When you are honored, you shall honor [others] in turn."
The rises and falls of the lords of men depend upon the planets; likewise, the existence and non-existence of the world depend on them. Therefore, the planets are most worthy of worship.
One should offer this hospitality even to the planets once a year;
endowed with health and strength, he shall live for a hundred autumns. (Chapter 13: The Duties of Kings, p. 107)
One who possesses great energy, is liberal, grateful, and serves his elders;
who is humble, endowed with courage, of noble birth, truthful in speech, and pure.
One who does not procrastinate, who possesses a retentive memory, who is not mean-spirited and likewise not harsh;
who is righteous, free from vices, wise, brave, and a knower of secrets.

A king should be a protector of his own vulnerabilities in the science of inquiry (ānvīkṣikī) as well as in the science of government (daṇḍanīti); furthermore, he should be disciplined in the science of economics (vārtā) and in the triple Vedas (trayī).
He should appoint ministers who are wise, hereditary, steadfast, and pure; with them, and then with a Brahmin, he should deliberate upon the affairs of the kingdom, and thereafter he himself.

He should appoint as his domestic priest one who is learned in the Vedas, well-born on both sides of his family, skilled in the science of statecraft (*daṇḍanīti*), and likewise proficient in the *Atharvāṅgirasa*.
For the sake of performing rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti,
he should indeed choose officiating priests (ṛtvij) and should likewise perform sacrifices according to the rules, accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
One should give enjoyments and various riches to the Brahmins;
for that which is bestowed upon Brahmins constitutes an inexhaustible treasure for kings.

O Brahmin, an oblation offered into the fire from the presence of another fire— provided it is not spilled, does not waver, and is not defiled by expiatory rites— is declared here to be the most excellent.
One should acquire what has not been acquired through righteous effort; what has been acquired, one should protect with diligence;
what has been protected, one should increase through prudent policy; and what has been increased, one should bestow upon worthy recipients.
Having given land or having established a fixed endowment (*nibandha*),
the king should cause a document to be prepared for the information of future benevolent rulers.
On a cloth or on a copper plate, marked with his own seal,
the lord of the earth shall have inscribed his own lineage and himself.
One should cause a stable edict to be made, complete with the dimensions of the land received, a description of the boundaries of the gift,
and the signature of one's own hand along with the date.

He should settle in a region that is pleasant, suitable for cattle, productive, and of the *jāṅgala* type; there he should construct fortresses for the protection of his people, his treasury, and himself.
And in each of those matters, he should appoint supervisors who are proficient, skillful, pure,
and diligent in the work of revenue, production, and expenditure.
There is no dharma for kings higher than this: that wealth acquired in battle is always given to Brahmins and security is granted to the subjects.
Those who are slain in battles for the sake of land while facing the enemy and not turning their backs,
go to heaven by means of non-deceptive weapons, just like yogins.
For those who do not retreat when their ranks are broken, the steps [they take] are equal to [the merit of] a sacrifice;
however, the king takes away the merit of those who are slain while fleeing.
One should not strike one who says "I am yours," a eunuch, one who is unarmed, one who has surrendered to another, one who has turned away from battle, or one who is watching a spectacle or the like.
Having ensured protection, he should rise and personally inspect income and expenditure;
then, having attended to legal matters and bathed, he may eat as he pleases.
He should deposit gold brought by messengers in the treasuries;
then, having consulted with his ministers, he should inspect the spies and dispatch envoys.
Thereafter, he may move about at his own pleasure, or remain in the company of his ministers; having inspected the troops, he should deliberate with the commander-in-chief.
Having performed the twilight devotions, he should listen to the secret speech of his spies;
he should enjoy himself with song and dance, and likewise recite his private Vedic study.
He should go to sleep to the sound of musical instruments and likewise wake up to that same sound;
he should contemplate the scriptures with his intellect, as well as all his duties.
Then he should respectfully dispatch spies among his own people and among others;
and he should be greeted with benedictions by the officiating priests, the family chaplain, and the teachers.
Having seen [them], he should give cows, gold, and land to those who know the luminaries (astronomers) and physicians;
thereafter, he should give houses and dwellings to those learned in the Vedas (śrotriyas).
Toward Brahmins he should be patient; toward his affectionate kin, straightforward; and toward his enemies, wrathful. Toward his circle of servants and his subjects, the king should be like a father.
By protecting [his subjects] according to the law, he takes a sixth part of their merit;
for the protection of his subjects is superior to all forms of giving.
He should protect the subjects who are being oppressed by rogues, thieves, evildoers, those who commit great acts of violence, and others— especially by scribes.
Whatever sin the subjects commit when they are not protected,
half of that belongs to the king, since he receives taxes from them.
Having learned through spies the conduct of those appointed to oversee the kingdom,
the king should honor the virtuous and put to death those who are the opposite.
Having deprived those who live by bribery of their wealth, he should banish them;
he should always cause those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) to dwell [in his realm], providing them with constant gifts, honors, and hospitality.
That king who, by unjust means, increases his own treasury at the expense of the kingdom, shall soon be deprived of his royal fortune and meet with destruction along with his kinsmen.
The fire produced from the suffering and distress of the subjects does not cease until it has consumed the lineage, the fortune, and the life-force of the king.
Whatever dharma belongs to a king in the protection of his own kingdom,
that very same dharma in its entirety he attains when bringing another's kingdom under his control.
In whatever country a particular custom, legal practice, or family tradition exists,
that very same practice must be maintained when it comes under one's control.
Since the kingdom has its root in counsel, he should therefore keep his counsel well-guarded,
so that others do not know it until the results of his actions have arisen.
The enemy, the friend, the neutral, the immediate neighbor, and the one beyond him—
this circle [of kings] should be considered in due order through the means of conciliation and the rest.
The means are conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and likewise force;
when properly employed, they may succeed, but force is the last resort when no other way remains.
He should properly employ these strategic means: peace, war, marching, halting, seeking refuge, and the double policy.
When the enemy kingdom is endowed with the excellence of crops, then he should march;
provided that the enemy is weakened while his own army and men are joyful and well-supplied with mounts.
The accomplishment of action is established upon both destiny and human effort;
therein, destiny is manifested as the human effort performed in a previous body.

Some wise men maintain that the fruit [of action] arises from destiny, others from inherent nature, some from time, and others from human effort; [still others] desire it to arise from the combination of these.
For just as a chariot cannot move with only one wheel,
so too destiny does not succeed without human effort.
Since the acquisition of friends is superior to the acquisition of gold and land,
one should therefore strive to attain that [acquisition of friends], remaining composed and guarding the truth.
The sovereign, the ministers, the people, the fort, the treasury, the army, and likewise the allies—these are the constituent elements; the kingdom is said to have seven limbs.
Having obtained that [kingly power], the king should inflict punishment upon those of evil conduct;
for Dharma was created by Brahmā in the form of punishment in ancient times.
He cannot be led away by justice by one who is greedy, of unrefined intellect, untruthful, impure, lacking good companions, or lacking wisdom.
When applied according to the scriptures, it gladdens the entire world—including gods, asuras, and humans; otherwise, it would provoke its wrath.
Unjust punishment destroys heaven, fame, and the world;
but for a king, proper punishment brings about heaven, fame, and victory.
Even a brother, a son, a worthy guest, a father-in-law, or even a maternal uncle— there is no one who, having deviated from his own duty, is not subject to punishment by the king.
That king who punishes those deserving of punishment and duly executes those deserving of death has,
by that act, performed sacrifices completed with excellent sacrificial fees.
Having reflected thus, the king, surrounded by his assessors, should personally examine the legal cases day by day, each yielding fruit equal to that of a sacrifice. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.360)
The king, having disciplined those who have deviated from their own duties— whether they be families, castes, guilds, or even local assemblies— should establish them on the right path.
A particle of dust moving in a sunbeam through a lattice is known as a *trasareṇu*;
eight of those make one *likṣā*, and three of those are called a *rājasarṣapa*.
Three *gaura* make one *yava*; three medium *yava* make one *kṛṣṇala*; five *kṛṣṇala* make one *māṣa*; and sixteen *māṣa* make one *suvarṇa*.
Four or even five suvarṇas are proclaimed to be one pala;
two kṛṣṇalas make a silver māṣa, and sixteen of those make a dharaṇa.
A *māna* consists of one hundred *dharaṇas*; ten *dharaṇas* indeed make a *pala*.
Four *suvarṇas* make a *niṣka*, while a copper *kārṣika* is a *paṇa*.
A fine of eighty thousand paṇas is called the highest amercement (uttamasāhasa);
half of that is declared the middle amercement (madhyama), and half of that again is remembered as the lowest amercement (adhama).
The punishment of censure, the punishment of speech, the punishment of fines, and likewise the punishment of corporal death—
these should be applied either individually or collectively, according to the nature of the offense.
Having ascertained the offense, the place, the time, and also the strength, as well as the age,
the action, and the wealth, he shall inflict punishment upon those deserving of punishment.
[End of the Chapter on Conduct]
[II. Chapter on Judicial Procedure] [1.
Section on the General Matrix of Judicial Procedure] Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.1a: The king shall examine judicial cases together with learned Brāhmaṇas.
In accordance with the treatises on dharma, he should be free from anger and greed.
The king should appoint as members of the court those who are accomplished in sacred learning and study, who know the Dharma, who speak the truth, and who are impartial toward both enemy and friend.
If, however, due to the demands of business, the king does not personally oversee legal proceedings,
he must appoint a Brāhmaṇa who knows all the laws to preside over them together with the members of the court.
Those members of the court who act contrary to the legal codes out of passion, greed, or even fear,
shall each be punished separately with a fine double the amount of the dispute.
When one who has not been oppressed by others through a path deviating from the Smṛtis and established custom brings a matter before the king, that indeed constitutes a ground for legal litigation.
In the presence of the defendant, the plaintiff shall cause a document to be written down exactly as it was stated,
marked with the year, month, fortnight, day, name, caste, and other identifying characteristics.

Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.7: After the meaning of the plaint has been heard, the defendant’s reply shall be written down in the presence of the plaintiff; thereafter, the plaintiff shall immediately cause to be written the proof for the matter he has asserted.
When that is established, one attains success; otherwise, the opposite occurs.
This four-footed judicial procedure has been set forth for legal disputes.

[2. Chapter on the Special Categories of Legal Procedure] Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.9: Without having fully resolved the charge brought against him, one should not bring a counter-charge against that person;
nor should one, by means of another, cause a person already charged to undergo a change in his statement.
In cases of mutual assault and in matters of violence, one may bring a counter-charge;
a surety capable of resolving the matter must be accepted from both parties.
If he denies it and is proven [guilty], he shall pay the debt to the king and an equal amount as a fine;
one who makes a false accusation shall pay double the amount of the claim.

In cases of violence, theft, verbal or physical assault, false accusations regarding a cow, or the violation of a woman, one should litigate immediately; in other matters, the time for litigation is said to depend on the parties' own desire.
He moves from one place to another,
licks the corners of his mouth, his forehead perspires, and his face turns pale.

When his speech becomes parched and faltering, when he speaks much that is contradictory, when he does not honor [the judge] with his voice or eyes, and when he also distorts his lips; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.14.
One who undergoes a change from his natural state through actions of mind, speech, or body—
whether during a formal accusation or while giving testimony— is proclaimed to be "corrupt."
He who, being independent, establishes a matter of doubtful meaning; he who departs [from court];
and he who, though summoned, says nothing—all such a person is declared by tradition to be defeated and liable to punishment.
When there are witnesses on both sides, the witnesses belong to the plaintiff;
but when the plaintiff's case has been refuted, they belong to the defendant.
If a dispute should involve a wager, the judge shall cause the loser to pay the fine,
his own wager, and the debt itself to the creditor.
Having set aside frivolous objections, the king should conduct legal proceedings on the basis of the truth;
for even the truth, if not presented, is lost in a lawsuit.

If a defendant denies a written document but is proven in one part of it, he must be made by the king to pay the entire amount; however, that which was not previously declared [in court] shall not be accepted as evidence.
When there is a conflict between two Smṛtis, reasoning is more powerful in legal proceedings;
however, it is established that the Dharmaśāstra is more powerful than the Arthaśāstra.
It is declared that documentary evidence, possession, and witnesses are the means of proof.
In the absence of any one of these, one of the divine ordeals is prescribed.
In all disputes concerning property, the subsequent legal act is stronger;
however, in the case of a mortgage, a gift, or a purchase, the prior act is more powerful.
For land, loss occurs after twenty years for one who sees it being enjoyed by another but does not speak out; for wealth, loss occurs after ten years.
Except for property consisting of pledges, boundary markers, deposits, and the wealth of the mentally disabled or minors;
likewise, except for the property of sealed deposits, the king, women, and Vedic scholars.
The king shall cause the one who misappropriates deposits and the like to pay the wealth to the creditor,
and a fine equal to that amount to the king, or otherwise according to his capacity.
Title-deed is superior to possession, except in the case of possession acquired through prior succession;
even a title-deed has no force at all where there is not even a small amount of possession.
But he by whom the title-deed was executed, being sued, must produce it;
neither his son nor his grandson need do so, for in that case possession is more weighty.
If one who has been accused is proven to have come from another [source], his heir shall recover that property;
in such a case, possession is not a valid ground when it is devoid of a legal title.
The king, his appointed officials, guilds, corporations, and then families— among these,
each preceding one is to be known as more authoritative than the following in the legal procedure for men.
He shall annul legal proceedings brought about by force or fraud,
as well as those conducted at night, inside a house, outside [the court], or by enemies.
A legal proceeding initiated by one who is intoxicated, insane, afflicted by illness, beset by calamity, a child, or terrified,
as well as one conducted by an incompetent person, is not valid.
Property lost and then found shall be returned by the king to the owner; if he cannot prove his ownership by signs, he deserves a fine equal to that property.
Upon finding a treasure-trove, the king shall give half to the twice-born;
however, a learned twice-born man may take the whole, since he is the master of all.
When a treasure is found by someone other than the rightful heir, the king shall take a sixth part of it;
if it was discovered without being reported, he shall be made to pay that same amount as a fine.
Property stolen by thieves must be restored by the king to the subject;
for if he does not restore it, he incurs the guilt of the owner of that property.
[3. Section on the Taking of Loans] Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.37: With a pledge, the interest shall be one-eightieth part [of the principal] month after month;
otherwise, according to the order of the castes, it shall be two, three, four, or five percent per hundred.
Those traveling through forests shall pay ten percent; those traveling by sea, twenty percent or one hundred percent;
or else, all [creditors] may take interest agreed upon by themselves, regardless of the species of the debtors.

The interest on livestock and female animals is eightfold at the maximum; that on liquids is eightfold at the maximum; and that on clothing, grain, and gold is fourfold, threefold, and twofold respectively at the maximum.

One who, having approached [the court], pursues his claim shall not be censured by the king. But one who, while his case is being pursued, goes to the king [himself] shall be punished and made to pay that debt.
A debtor should be made to pay the creditors according to the order in which they presented their claims; however, after that, he must first pay the king and then the Brāhmaṇas.
The king shall cause the debtor to pay ten percent on the amount recovered;
and the creditor who has obtained his money shall be made to pay five percent.
One may compel a man of lower caste who is impoverished to perform labor for the sake of the debt;
however, a Brāhmaṇa who is impoverished should be made to pay gradually, according to his income.
If one does not accept one's own wealth when it is being offered, having been lent and deposited with a neutral third party, it shall not increase beyond that point.
If a debt has been contracted for the sake of the family by those who have not yet divided the inheritance,
the heirs shall pay it when the head of the household has died or gone abroad.
A father shall not pay a debt contracted by his wife, his son, or by his son;
likewise, a husband shall not pay a debt contracted by his wife, except for what was incurred for the sake of the household.

A son shall not pay, on behalf of his father, debts incurred through drinking liquor, gambling, or lawsuits; nor the remainder of fines or tolls; nor gifts made for no purpose; nor such debts here as are not paternal.
The husband shall pay the debt of the wives of a cowherd, a vintner, an actor, a washerman, or a hunter,
because their livelihood depends upon him.
A woman must pay a debt that was contracted by her with her husband's consent, or one that she herself incurred; she is not liable for any other debt.
When the father has gone abroad, is deceased, or is overwhelmed by calamity,
the debt must be paid by the sons or grandsons, provided it is established by witnesses in the event of a denial.

The inheritor of the estate shall be made to pay the debt, as shall the one who takes the wife; likewise, the son whose wealth has not been entrusted to another shall pay for his father who leaves no heir.
Furthermore, among brothers, between husband and wife, and between father and son,
