suretyship, debt, and witness testimony are not prescribed when they have not yet divided their inheritance.
Suretyship is prescribed for appearance, for confidence, and for payment.
However, if the first two [types of surety] fail, the debt must be paid; in the case of the other, even the sons must pay.

If the guarantor for appearance (*darśana-pratibhū*) or the guarantor for confidence (*prātyayika*) has died, his sons shall not pay that debt; however, they must pay the debt of one who stood as a guarantor for payment (*dāna*).

If there are many sureties who pay the debt with their own respective shares, they shall do so among themselves; however, when they have resorted to a single liability, the creditor may collect from them as he pleases.
But whatever wealth a surety is compelled to pay publicly to the creditor,
that shall be doubled and must be repaid by the debtors to him.
Interest on female slaves and cattle is simply the offspring; on grain, it is threefold;
clothing is declared to be fourfold; and likewise, liquids are eightfold.
A pledge shall be forfeited when the debt has doubled, if it is not redeemed;
a pledge for use shall be lost with the lapse of time, but one that yields fruit is never lost.
In the case of the use of a pledge for which protection was required, there is no interest; likewise, if it is damaged or lost, [the debtor must compensate].
That which is lost or destroyed—except through acts of God or the king—must be restored.

The validity of a pledge is established through its acceptance; even if it is being protected, if it reaches a state of worthlessness, another pledge may be taken, or the creditor shall become the owner of the property.
He shall cause the debtor to pay the principal with interest for that which was made by means of a pledge or a bond;
however, he shall cause the payment of double the value for that which was made by way of a formal agreement (*satyakāra*).
When the debtor has arrived [to redeem it], the pledge must be released; otherwise, he would become a thief.
If the creditor is absent, he should deposit the money with a local family and take possession of the pledge.
Or it may remain there at its value fixed at that time, without interest;
or even without the debtor's consent, the creditor may sell it in the presence of witnesses.
But when the debt has become double on account of the pledge, then indeed—once the money produced from it has entered and reached the amount of double the debt—the pledge must be released.
(Section 4: On Deposits)

When an object placed in a container is handed over into the hand of another without being described, that object is termed *aupanidhika* (a sealed deposit); it must be returned in exactly the same manner.
He shall not be made to pay for what has been stolen by the king, by fate, or by thieves;
however, if it is not recovered despite being sought, he shall be made to pay [the value] and a fine equal to that amount.
If one makes a living by his own will [using another's property], he shall be punished and made to pay that [property] along with its interest.
This same rule applies to things borrowed, entrusted for delivery, deposits, and pledges.
[Chapter 5: On Witnesses]
Those who practice austerity, are disposed toward giving, are of noble birth, speak the truth,
prioritize righteousness, are upright, have sons, and are endowed with wealth.

Witnesses should be known as at least three in number, devoted to the performance of rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti; they are traditionally held to be either all of the same caste and class as the parties, or all of any caste and class.
Women, children, the elderly, gamblers, those intoxicated, the insane, the accused; performers on stage, heretics, forgers, and those with impaired senses.
An outcast, a relative, one interested in the matter, an associate, an enemy, a thief,
one who commits violence, and one whose fault has been observed— these, including those previously mentioned such as the "expelled," are not to be admitted as witnesses.
A single person who knows the law may be a witness if he is approved by both parties.
In cases of adultery, theft, verbal abuse, and violence, everyone may be a witness.
He should cause the witnesses—who stand in the presence of the plaintiff and the defendant—to hear [the following]:
"Those worlds which are for those who commit minor sins, as well as for those who commit great sins;
those worlds which belong to arsonists, and those which belong to the killers of women and children."
He who gives false testimony incurs all of those [sins].
Whatever merit has been performed by you over hundreds of previous births,
know that all of it belongs to him whom you defeat through falsehood.
For a man who fails to give testimony regarding a debt shall be made by the king to pay the entire amount along with a ten-percent fine on the forty-sixth day.
For that lowest of men who, though knowing the facts, does not give testimony,
is indeed equal to false witnesses in both his sin and his punishment.
In a conflict between two witnesses, the testimony of the majority prevails; likewise, when the numbers are equal, the testimony of those possessing superior qualities prevails.
But when there is a conflict even among those of superior qualities, the testimony of those who are the most excellent in virtue must be accepted.
He whose witnesses declare his claim to be true shall be the victor;
for him who speaks otherwise, defeat is certain.
Even when testimony has been given by witnesses, if other witnesses who are more virtuous,
or twice as numerous, should state otherwise, the former witnesses are considered false.
The forger and the false witnesses shall each be punished separately;
the fine shall be double the amount in dispute, though a Brāhmaṇa is ordained to be banished.
He who, having been made to hear the testimony by others, denies it, being enveloped in darkness—him one shall cause to pay a fine eightfold; but a Brāhmaṇa, however, one shall banish.
Where the death penalty for members of the [four] castes would otherwise result, there one may speak untruth as witness;
to purify that [sin], the twice-born must offer a *sārasvata* oblation of boiled rice (*caru*). (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.83) [Section 6:
On Written Documents] (pp. 190–191)
Whatever matter has been settled between two parties by their own mutual consent,
a document should be executed for that purpose, provided it contains witnesses and begins with the name of the creditor.
[The gift] should be marked by the year, month, half-month, day, name, caste, and one's own lineage (gotra), as well as by the name of one's fellow student, oneself, and one's father.
When the matter is concluded, the debtor shall write with his own hand:
"What is written above is my assent as the son of so-and-so."
The witnesses, with their own hands, preceded by the names of their fathers, should write: "I, so-and-so, am a witness here. Thus they are instructed.
"Requested by both parties, this has been written by me, the son of so-and-so, by such-and-such a person"—
thus the scribe should write at the end.
Even without witnesses, a document written in one's own hand is declared to be valid evidence, provided it was not executed through force or fraud.
A debt contracted by means of a written document is to be paid by only three generations of persons;
however, the pledge is enjoyed as long as that debt has not been repaid.
If a document is located in another country, is illegible, lost, erased, stolen,
broken, burnt, or torn, one should have another document executed.
The purification of a doubtful document shall be established by means of a signature in one's own hand and the like,
as well as by reason, probability, performance, marks, connection, and title-deeds.
The debtor, having paid the money, should write on the back of the document;
or the creditor, having received it, should provide a receipt marked with his own hand.

Having paid the debt, one should tear up the document, or else have another document executed for the sake of clearing the account; or whatever debt was evidenced by witnesses must be repaid in the presence of witnesses. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.94) [7.
Section on Ordeals]
The balance, fire, water, poison, and the ordeal by sacred libation are the divine ordeals for the purpose of purification in this world;
these are employed in cases of serious accusation when the accuser is prepared to undergo the penalty himself.
Or, by mutual consent, one may act as the debtor and the other as the guarantor for the head.
Even without a guarantor for the head, one may act so in cases of treason against the king or in the event of a mortal sin.
Having summoned him who has fasted since sunrise and bathed with his clothes on,
the king shall cause all the ordeals to be performed in the presence of Brahmins.
For women, children, the elderly, the blind, the lame, Brāhmaṇas, and the sick, the ordeal shall be by the balance;
for a Śūdra, by fire or water; or for [anyone], the seven grains of poison.

One should not employ a ploughshare, nor poison, nor a balance for less than a thousand [paṇas]. However, in matters concerning the king and in cases of formal accusation, these may always be used by those who are pure.
One who is accused should resort to the balance, held by experts in the art of weighing.
Having become level with the counterweight, it was lowered after drawing a line.
O Tula, you were created of old by the gods as the abode of truth;
therefore, speak the truth, O auspicious one, and release me from my doubt.
"O Mother, if I am a doer of evil, then lead me downward;
if I am pure, lead me upward"—with these words he should consecrate the balance.
Having observed that the two hands have crushed grains of rice,
one should then place seven leaves of the *aśvattha* tree upon them and wrap them with a thread.
O Agni, Purifier, you move within all beings;
O Sage, like a witness, declare the truth to me regarding my merits and sins.
When he has spoken thus, [the judge] shall place a smooth iron ball weighing fifty palas and glowing with fire upon both of his hands.
Taking that [fire], he should walk slowly for exactly seven circles;
each circle should be known to be sixteen finger-breadths in diameter, with an equal interval between them.
Having released the fire, one whose rice-grains have been crushed but who has not been burned shall attain purification;
if the ball falls in between, or if there is doubt, he shall take it up again.
Having sworn an oath over water with the words, "O Varuṇa, protect me by means of truth," [he shall drink].
Standing in water reaching up to the navel, one should enter the water after grasping the thighs.

Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.109ab: When another swift man has brought back an arrow that was shot at the same moment [the ordeal began], Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.109cd: if one should see the person with their limbs submerged [in the water] after that [arrow] has gone, they shall attain purification.
Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.110a: O Poison, you are the son of Brahmā, established in truth and dharma.
"Protect me from this curse; by truth, become nectar for me."
Having spoken thus, he should consume the Śārṅga poison, which originates from the snowy mountains;
if it is digested without its characteristic effects, one should declare that person to be pure.
Having worshipped the fierce deities, one should take the water used for their ablutions;
having poured it out, one should then cause [the person] to drink three handfuls of that water.
If a terrible calamity caused by a king or by fate occurs for anyone within fourteen days [of the ordeal], he shall be considered pure; of this there is no doubt. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.113)

[8. The Section on the Division of Inheritance] (p.216) Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.114: If the father should make a division, he may divide the sons according to his will; or he may give the eldest a superior share, or all may be equal sharers. (p.220) Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.114c: Or the eldest may receive a distinguished portion, or they may all be equal in their shares.
If [the father] should divide [the estate] into equal shares, the wives should be made sharers of an equal portion,
provided that no woman's property (*strīdhana*) has been given to them by the husband or by the father-in-law.
If one who is capable does not desire [to share], a separate partition may be made after giving him something;
for those whose shares were divided unequally, the partition made by the father is declared to be lawful.
After the death of both parents, the sons shall divide the inheritance and the debt equally.

The daughters [shall take] the remainder of the mother's estate after the debt; in their absence, the lineage [inherits]. Whatever else has been acquired by oneself without detriment to the paternal property [is to be divided among the sons].
That which is given as a friendly gift or for the sake of marriage shall not belong to the heirs.
If one recovers property that had been stolen but had come into his possession by succession, he need not give it to his co-heirs; the same applies to what has been acquired through learning.
When property is acquired for the common benefit, the division is ordained to be equal;
however, for those who have multiple fathers, the allotment of shares is determined according to the fathers.
Whether it be land acquired by the grandfather, or a leasehold, or even property itself—
in such cases, the ownership of the father and the son is indeed equal.
A son born after the partition of the estate from a wife of equal caste is entitled to a share;
or rather, his share shall be determined from the visible assets, after deducting the income and expenses.
Whatever has been given by both parents shall belong to that [son] alone. When the sons divide the inheritance after the father's death, the mother also shall take an equal share.
But those who have not been consecrated should be consecrated by their brothers who have already been consecrated;
and the sisters, having been given a fourth part from their own share, [should likewise be consecrated].
The sons of a Brāhmaṇa, according to their respective castes, shall receive four, three, two, and one shares;
those born of a Kṣatriya shall receive three, two, and one shares; and those born of a Vaiśya shall receive two and one shares.
If property that was mutually misappropriated is discovered after the partition has been made, they shall divide it again into equal shares; such is the settled rule.
A son begotten through the practice of *niyoga* by a man who has no son upon the wife of another is,
according to the law, the heir to the estate and the offerer of the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) to both fathers.

The legitimate son (aurasa) is born of the lawful wife; equal to him is the son of an appointed daughter (putrikā-suta). The son of the field (kṣetraja), however, is one begotten upon the wife by a man of the same lineage or by another.
A son born secretly in the house is known as a *gūḍhaja* (secretly born);
one born of an unmarried girl is considered a *kānīna*, the son of his maternal grandfather.
A son born to a woman who has been previously married, whether she be unwidowed or widowed, is a *paunarbhava*.
A son whom a mother or a father gives away becomes an *adopted* (*dattaka*) son.
One who is purchased from them is called "purchased" (*krīta*); one who is made by himself is "artificial" (*kṛtrima*).
One who gives himself away is "self-given" (*svayaṃdatta*); one conceived in the womb and brought forth together [with the bride] is "born together with the bride" (*sahoḍhaja*).
He who is taken up after having been abandoned is an *apaviddha* son;
among these [types of sons], each subsequent one offers the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) and inherits the share in the absence of the preceding one.
This rule regarding sons of the same caste has been declared by me for [sons born of] wives;
even one born of a Śūdra woman through a Śūdra husband shall, if born of desire, be a sharer of a portion.
When the father has died, the brothers shall make him a recipient of half a share.
A man without brothers shall take the entire inheritance, except for the son of a daughter.
The wife, the daughters, the parents, the brothers,
their sons, the agnates, the kinsmen, the pupils, and those who have lived as religious students (sabrahmacārin).
In the absence of these, each subsequent one among them becomes the heir to the wealth of the preceding.
For this rule applies to all castes regarding one who has died without a son.
The heirs to the property of forest-dwellers (vānaprasthas), ascetics (yatis), and students (brahmacārins) are, respectively:
the teacher (ācārya), the virtuous disciple (sat-śiṣya), the spiritual brother (dharma-bhrātṛ), and the fellow ascetic (eka-tīrthin). (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.137)

But a reunited coparcener shall take the share of one who has reunited, and a uterine brother that of another uterine brother; he shall give the share to one born [after reunion] and take the share of one who dies [during reunion].
But a uterine brother who is reunited shall take the wealth, not one who is not uterine;
or even one who is not reunited may take it, but not one born of a different mother who is merely reunited.
A eunuch, one who has fallen from caste, his offspring, one who is lame, one who is insane,
one who is mentally dull, the blind, and those afflicted with incurable diseases— these should be maintained by the family, but they shall receive no share of the inheritance.
Among these, the legitimate sons (*aurasa*) and those born of the wife (*kṣetraja*), being free from defects, are entitled to inherit their shares;
and their daughters must be maintained until they are provided for by their husbands.
The childless wives of these [deceased brothers] must be maintained if they are of virtuous conduct;
likewise, those who are unchaste or hostile should be banished.
That which is given by her father, mother, husband, or brother; that which is received at the nuptial fire;
and that which is given on account of supersession, and so forth, is declared to be the woman's property (strīdhana).
Likewise, property given by a kinsman, a nuptial gift (*śulka*), and even a subsequent gift (*anvādheyaka*)—
if she dies childless, her kinsmen shall obtain that.
The property of a woman who dies without offspring belongs to her husband even in the case of the four [marriages] beginning with the Brāhma;
however, among the remaining [marriages], if she has borne children, it goes to her daughters, and if not, it goes to her father.
Having given away a daughter, one who takes her back should be punished and must pay the expenses along with interest;
if she has died, he may take back what was given after deducting the expenses incurred by both parties.
In times of famine, for religious duties, during illness, or when there is imprisonment,
the husband is not obliged to return the woman's property that he has taken from her.
One should give an equal amount as an *ādhivedanika* gift to a wife who has been superseded by another;
however, if no such wealth was previously given to her, one should provide half of that amount once it has been given.

In a dispute concerning a partition, the determination of the partition is to be known through kinsmen, relatives, witnesses, written records, and separate houses, fields, and personal property. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.149) [9.
Section on Disputes Concerning Boundaries] (p. 255)
In a dispute concerning the boundary of a field, the neighbors, elders, and others, the herdsmen, the farmers living along the boundary, and all those who frequent the forest shall be witnesses.
They shall mark the boundary by means of mounds, charcoal, husks, and trees,
as well as by dikes, anthills, depressions, bones, shrines, and other such signs.
Alternatively, four, eight, or even ten neighboring villagers from the same village,
wearing red garlands and garments, shall carry the boundary markers while supporting the earth.
But for falsehood, they shall each be punished by the king with the middle amercement.
In the absence of witnesses and identifying marks, the king is the establisher of the boundary.
In the case of groves, temples, villages, watering places, gardens, and dwellings—
this same rule is to be understood as applying to rainwater, flowing streams, and the like.
In cases of breaking a boundary marker, as well as in the transgression of a boundary,
and likewise in the seizure of a field, the punishments are the lowest, the highest, and the middle.
A dam that causes little harm but brings about beneficial results should not be prohibited;
likewise, a well that occupies another's land is not forbidden if it yields much water for one's own small field.
If one constructs an irrigation channel on a field without first informing the owner, the produce belongs to the owner;
in his absence, it belongs to the king.

If a person neither cultivates nor causes to be cultivated a field that has been struck by the plough, he shall be made to pay the fruit of the cultivation and have the field cultivated by another. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.158) [Section on Disputes between Owner and Herdsman] (p. 261)
A female buffalo that destroys crops shall be fined eight māṣas;
a cow shall be fined half of that, and a goat or sheep half of that again.
If they sit down after having eaten [the fodder], the fine shall be double that which has been prescribed;
this same rule applies even in the case of a pasture, including donkeys, camels, and buffaloes.
As long as the crop perishes, so long shall the fruit belong to the owner of the field;
the cowherd is to be beaten, but the owner of the cow deserves the previously mentioned fine.
There is no offense in a field located on a path or at the edge of a village pasture; however, if one acts intentionally, he deserves punishment like that of a thief.

Large bulls, animals set free, those that have recently calved, those that are traveling, and so forth— those for which there is no keeper need not be made liable [for damage], provided they have been overtaken by divine or royal calamities.
Just as a cowherd should return the cattle entrusted to him in the evening,
so too a hired laborer must be made to pay for those that have died or been lost through negligence.
But when damage occurs due to the fault of the keeper, a fine is prescribed for the keeper:
twelve and a half paṇas, as well as the value of the property itself for the owner.
Cattle may graze according to the will of the village folk or by the authority of the king;
furthermore, a twice-born man may take grass, firewood, and flowers from anywhere at all times.
The distance between fields in a village shall be one hundred *dhanus* in circumference;
for a market town (*kharvaṭa*) it shall be two hundred, and for a city (*nagara*) four hundred. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.167) [Chapter 11: Sale Without Ownership] (p. 265)
One may recover one's own property sold by another; however, the fault lies with the purchaser if it was not openly declared.
One who buys from a low person in secret, for a low price, or at an improper time, is a thief.
Having discovered someone who has stolen or lost property, one should cause that person to be apprehended;
and if there is a lapse in time or place, one should seize the offender oneself and hand him over.
Purification from the charge comes from the production of the seller; the owner recovers the property, and the king receives a fine.
The buyer recovers the price from him who was the seller of that [property].
A lost property may be recovered through legal title or through possession; otherwise, if it is not proven by the claimant, he shall pay a fine of five times its value to the king.
He who recovers from the hand of another property that has been stolen or lost,
without having reported it to the king, shall be fined ninety-six *paṇas*.
If property that has been lost or stolen is recovered by customs officials or guards of the station, the owner may take it back within one year; after that, the king shall take it.
For a single-hoofed animal, one should pay four *paṇas*; for a human, five;
for buffaloes, camels, and cows, two each; and for goats and sheep, one-quarter each. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.174)

One's own wealth may be given away without detriment to one's family, except for one's wife and sons; however, when there is a lineage remaining, one must not give away one's entire estate, nor that which has already been promised to another.
The acceptance of a gift should be public, especially in the case of immovable property. What has been promised as a gift, once given, must not be taken back again. [13.
Section on Regret after Purchase]
The examination of seeds, iron, draft animals, gems, women, milch cattle, and men shall take ten, one, five, seven days, a month, three days, and half a month respectively.
Gold is not diminished when melted in fire; silver loses two palas per hundred;
tin and lead lose eight palas per hundred, and copper fifteen palas per hundred. Iron loses ten palas per hundred.
On woolen cloth, cotton, and silk, the interest for a hundred [units] is ten palas;
for medium quality, the interest is five palas, while for fine quality, it is considered to be three palas.
In the case of woven silk and woolen cloth, a loss of one-thirtieth is recognized;
however, there is neither loss nor increase in the case of silken garments and bark-cloth.

Having ascertained the place, the time, and the possession, as well as the strength and weakness in the case of a lost item, those who are experts in matters of property shall declare what must be paid without doubt. [End of Section 14:
Non-compliance after Agreement]
One who has been made a slave by force, as well as one sold by thieves,
is liberated [from slavery] by saving the life of his master, by abandoning his food, or by the payment of a ransom for him.

One who has abandoned the life of a wandering ascetic becomes the king’s slave until death. Slavery is permitted for the social classes in the direct order of precedence, but not in the inverse order.
Even one who has mastered a craft shall reside in the house of the teacher for a fixed period;
as an apprentice, he shall receive his food from the teacher and deliver to him the fruits of his labor.
[15. Section on the Breach of Agreement]
Having established a residence in the city and appointed Brāhmaṇas there, the king should provide them with a livelihood and say: "Let your own dharma be protected."
But that which is established by convention (*samayika*) without contradicting one's own duty (*nija-dharma*),
as well as that law enacted by the king— both of these must be protected with effort.
But he who misappropriates the property of a corporation or violates its agreement,
having had all his property confiscated, the king shall banish him from the realm.
The instruction of those who speak for the welfare of the community must be followed by all;
whoever therein acts contrarily shall be made to pay the first fine.

The lord of the earth, having honored those who have come for the business of the assembly with gifts, marks of respect, and hospitality, should dismiss them once their business is accomplished. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.189)
One who has been dispatched for the business of a corporate body shall deliver whatever he may obtain;
if he does not deliver it himself, he shall be made to pay eleven times its value.
Those who know the law, who are pure and free from greed, shall be the deliberators on affairs; their word must be carried out when they speak for the welfare of the community.
This same rule applies to guilds, merchants, heretics, and assemblies;
the king shall protect them from internal dissension and preserve their traditional customs.
(Chapter 16: On the Payment of Wages)
If a laborer who has received wages abandons his work, he shall be made to pay double;
if he has not received wages, he shall be made to pay an equal amount, and the tools must be protected for the sake of the servants.
But he who causes work to be done without having fixed the wages must be made to pay a tenth part of the profits from trade, cattle,
or crops by the king.

If one should miss the proper place and time, or should effect the acquisition otherwise, in that case it shall be at the pleasure of the owner; if more than the usual amount has been produced, the surplus must be given.

Whatever amount of work one performs, that much shall be his wages. If the task is impossible for either party to accomplish, [the wage is forfeited]; but if it is accomplished, one should pay according to what was agreed.
If goods are lost due to causes other than the king or an act of God, the driver shall be made to pay for them;
likewise, one who causes an obstruction to the departure shall be made to pay double the wages.
If he abandons a servant who has set out on a journey, he must pay him one-seventh of his wages; if on the road, one-fourth;
and if half-way home, the full amount. The same applies to one who causes him to abandon his service.
(Chapter 17: Gambling and Betting)
In a gambling match where the interest on the stake is one hundredfold,
the keeper of the gaming house shall take five percent from a dishonest gambler and ten percent from any other.
Having been properly protected, he shall give the king the share as previously determined.
He should cause the winner to take possession of what was won and, being patient, shall give truthful testimony.

When the king's share has been received and the assembly of gamblers is well-known, he should cause the winner to pay the stake in a place where there is a presiding official; otherwise, he shall not do so.
For they alone are the observers of legal proceedings and the witnesses;
therefore, those who play with false dice or by fraud should be banished by the king along with their marks.
Gambling should be conducted with a single stake for the purpose of identifying thieves;
this same rule is to be understood as applicable to betting with living creatures and to duels.
[18. Section on Verbal Abuse]
If one mocks those who are deficient in limbs, senses, or afflicted by disease with praises that are true, false, or otherwise distorted,
he shall be fined twelve and a half paṇas.
If one swears, "I shall violate your sister or your mother," the king should compel that person to pay a fine of twenty-five [paṇas].

In cases of unrighteous acts, the fine shall be doubled for women who are others' wives and for those of the highest castes; thus should the infliction of punishment be carried out according to the relative superiority or inferiority of the social classes and birth.
In cases of defamation involving the reverse order of castes, the fines shall be double and triple [respectively];
for the castes in the direct order, they shall be reduced by half and half again from that amount.
In cases of verbal injury involving the destruction of the arms, neck, eyes, or thighs, the fine shall be as prescribed;
for injuries to the feet, nose, ears, hands, and so forth, the fine shall be half of that.
But one who is unable [to pay] and speaks thus should be fined ten *paṇas*.
Likewise, one who is able should be made to provide a surety for his security.
For an insult involving a crime causing loss of caste (*pātaka*), the punishment is the middle amercement;
however, for one associated with a minor offense (*upapātaka*), he shall be made to pay the first amercement.

Insulting those learned in the three Vedas, a king, or a deity is the highest amercement; insulting a caste or a guild is the middle amercement; and insulting a village or a district is the first amercement. (Chapter 19: On Assault)

But a legal dispute involving forged evidence, arising from fear, must be examined through marks, circumstantial reasoning, and documentary proof when there are no witnesses. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.212)
A fine of ten paṇas is prescribed for touching ashes, mud, or dust;
for touching impure substances, the heel, or spittle, the fine is double that amount.
In the case of women of equal status, the punishment is the same; however, it is double for those of higher status.
For women of lower status, the punishment is half; there is no punishment when [the act] is committed through delusion, intoxication, and the like.
The limb of a non-Brāhmaṇa that causes pain to a Brāhmaṇa shall be cut off;
however, if he merely raises his hand, the first amercement is the punishment, and if he actually touches him, half of that.
If one merely brandishes a hand or a foot, the fines shall be ten and twenty paṇas respectively;
but for all [offenses] involving a weapon against one another, the middle amercement applies.
For pulling at the feet, hair, or garment, or for seizing the hand, the fine shall be ten paṇas;
for causing pain, tearing a garment, wrapping around the feet, or stepping upon them, the punishment is one hundred paṇas.
A man who causes pain with wood or other materials without drawing blood shall be fined thirty-two paṇas; if blood is seen, the fine shall be doubled.
In the case of breaking a hand or a foot, or cutting off the ear or the nose, the middle amercement is the punishment;
likewise for causing a wound that breaks the skin, or for striking someone who is nearly dead.
In cases of obstructing movement, food, or speech; piercing the eyes or other [sensitive parts];
and breaking the neck, arms, or thighs, the middle amercement shall be imposed.
For many who kill a single person, the fine shall be double that which has been prescribed.
Property seized during a quarrel must be returned, and the fine shall be double that amount.
He who causes pain shall be made to pay the expenses incurred for its removal,
as well as the fine prescribed for that particular quarrel.
In cases of striking, cutting, piercing, or causing a wall to collapse,
one should be made to pay five, ten, or twenty paṇas, as well as the cost of repairing that damage.
One who casts into a house property that causes pain, or likewise something life-threatening, shall be made to pay sixteen *paṇas* for the first offense; for the second, the middle amercement.
In the case of causing pain, drawing blood, or likewise cutting off a limb or a member [of small animals],
the fine for small animals shall be two panas and upwards in successive order.
In the case of cutting off a male organ or causing death, the middle amercement shall be imposed, as well as the value [of the animal];
for large animals, the fine in these instances is double.
For cutting branches,
trunks, or the entire body of trees that bear shoots, and for trees that provide a livelihood, the fine is double that of twenty [paṇas].
In the case of trees growing near a sacred mound, a cremation ground, a boundary, a holy site, or a temple,
as well as for a tree of renown, the fine is double.
For the cutting of shrubs, clusters, bushes, creepers, spreading plants, medicinal herbs, and climbing plants, the fine shall be half of that prescribed previously for the aforementioned locations.
[End of Chapter 20: On Violence]
The forcible seizure of common property is declared to be *sāhasa* (violence).
The fine for this is twice the value of that property; however, if there is denial, it is fourfold.
He who causes another to commit *sāhasa* shall be made to pay double the fine.
And he who, having spoken thus, "I am the giver," should cause [the gift] to be performed, shall incur a fourfold [penalty].

One who rejects or transgresses the guest-offering (*arghya*), one who strikes his brother's wife, one who fails to deliver a entrusted message, and one who breaks a house by the sea; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.232.
For one who commits an injury against neighbors, family members, and others,
the settled rule is that the fine shall be fifty paṇas for each of them.
One who approaches a widow of his own accord, one who does not come to the rescue when a cry for help is raised, one who raises a false cry for help,
and a Caṇḍāla who touches members of the highest castes— [these shall be punished].
One who feeds Śūdras or renunciants at a rite for the gods or the ancestors is unfit;
likewise, one who administers an improper oath or performs the duties of an unworthy person is unfit.
One who obstructs the virility of a bull or small livestock, one who denies a common property, and one who causes the destruction of a maidservant's fetus; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.236.
Father, son, sister, brother, husband and wife, and teacher and pupil— among these, one who abandons another who has not fallen from grace shall be subject to a fine of one hundred [paṇas].
A laundryman who wears another's garment shall be fined three *paṇas*;
however, for selling, hiring out, pledging, or borrowing it, he shall be fined ten *paṇas*.
In a dispute between a father and a son, the fine for witnesses is three paṇas;
and for anyone who stands between them, the fine shall be eight times that amount.
One who forges scales, royal edicts, measures, or coins,
as well as anyone who deals with such forged items, shall be made to pay the highest fine.
He who declares a genuine coin to be counterfeit, or a counterfeit coin to be genuine—
that examiner of coins shall be made to pay the highest fine.
A physician who practices falsely shall be fined the first amercement for treating animals,
the middle amercement for humans, and the highest amercement for royal officers.
He who binds one who should not be bound, he who releases one who is bound,
and he who deals with one who has not attained legal majority, shall be made to pay the highest fine.
Whoever should take even an eighth part [of the value] by means of a measure or a scale,
he shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred [paṇas], as determined according to the increase or decrease [in value].
If one adulterates medicinal herbs, oils, salt, perfumes, grains, molasses,
and other such commodities with inferior substances, he shall be made to pay a fine of sixteen paṇas.
For one who falsely designates the genus of clay, leather, gems, thread, iron, wood, bark,
or cloth when they are not of that genus, the fine for selling such items is eightfold.
For one who brings about the exchange of a casket or the sale of counterfeit goods containing valuable articles, the determination of punishment shall be made according to the circumstances.

For damage to an article worth one paṇa, the fine is fifty; for one worth two paṇas, it is said to be one hundred. For articles of higher value, the fine increases in proportion to the increase in price.
For those artisans and craftsmen who, acting in concert, fix a price that is too high,
or who knowingly cause a decrease or increase in the price, the highest fine shall be imposed.
For merchants who, acting in concert, obstruct the sale of merchandise by fixing an improper price,
or for those who sell it [in such a manner], the prescribed punishment is the highest fine.
The price established by the king every day shall be used for the sale or the purchase [of goods];
from that proceeds the profit of the merchants, which is declared to be their rightful gain.
A merchant dealing in goods from his own country may take five percent;
however, he who buys and sells goods from a foreign land immediately must take ten percent.

Having established the expenses arising from the merchandise upon the price of the goods, the value should be fixed in a manner that provides favor to both the buyer and the seller. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.253) [Chapter 21:
The Section on Non-Delivery after Sale] (p. 298)
If one who has received the price does not deliver the merchandise to the purchaser,
he shall be made to pay that with interest, or the profit realized from the direction from which it was brought, if it has arrived from abroad.
Even if it has been sold, it may be resold if the previous buyer does not take possession;
for if the loss occurs due to the fault of the buyer, that loss shall belong to the buyer alone.
If a commodity is damaged due to an injury caused by the king or by fate,
the loss belongs solely to the seller who, having been asked for it, fails to deliver it.
If one sells an item in the hand of another, or sells what is defective as if it were non-defective,
the fine in that case shall be twice the value of the item.

A merchant who, without knowing the depreciation or appreciation of his merchandise, has no right of repentance after having purchased it; if he exercises such a right, he shall be liable to a fine of one-sixth.
[Chapter on Joint Undertakings] (p. 300)
When merchants perform work for the sake of profit through a partnership,
the gain or loss shall be according to the capital invested, or as determined by their agreement.
If a deposit is lost through negligence—whether it was forbidden [from being used] or not specifically entrusted—the owner shall restore it;
furthermore, from what is recovered after a disaster, he shall receive a tenth share as his fee for protection.
The king shall take a twentieth part as toll from the offering of goods for sale;
however, that which is sold while being obstructed by the king, or that which is fit for the king’s use, shall go to the king.
One who falsely states the quantity [of goods], one who evades the customs station,
and one who engages in fraudulent buying or selling, shall be made to pay eight times [the value].
A ferryman who collects toll for goods transported by land shall be made to pay ten paṇas;
this same penalty applies for failing to invite Brāhmaṇas and neighboring residents [to a feast].
When a person has died while traveling in a foreign land, his heirs, kinsmen, or relatives shall take the property; if they have not arrived, the king shall take it.
They should abandon one who acts crookedly or fails to provide the profit; if unable to do so, he should have it performed by another.
By this rule, the procedure for officiating priests, cultivators, and laborers has been declared.
[End of Section 23 on Theft] (p. 303)
A thief is apprehended by pursuers either through stolen property or by his footprints;
likewise, one who has previously committed a crime and one who wears impure clothing [is apprehended].
Others also are to be apprehended on suspicion through the concealment of their caste, name, and so forth;
as well as those addicted to gambling, women, and drink, and those with parched or distorted faces and voices.

Those who inquire about the property and houses of others while moving about in secret, those who have no income yet have many expenditures, and those who sell goods that have been lost or destroyed; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.268.
If one who has been apprehended on suspicion of theft does not clear himself,
the king, after making him restore the stolen property, shall punish him with the same penalty as a thief.
Having compelled the thief to restore what was stolen, the king shall execute him by various means of corporal punishment;
however, having branded a Brāhmaṇa with a mark, he shall banish him from his own kingdom.
If cattle are killed or stolen within the village boundary and have not yet left, the blame falls on the village headman;
but if it occurs on the road outside the boundary, the blame falls on the superintendent of the pasture or the officer who guards against thieves.
The village itself should provide [the boundary marker] within its own territory, or at the place where the footstep falls;
or else, five villages beyond the *krośa*, or even ten villages.
Men who capture bards, those who carry off horses and elephants,
and those who kill by force, he shall cause to be impaled upon stakes.
Those who commit robbery by snatching or those who break open a knot [of goods] shall have a hand and a thumb cut off;
for a second offense, they shall be deprived of one hand and one foot.
In cases of seizing property that is small, middling, or large, the punishment shall be determined according to its value;
in the administration of punishment, one must carefully consider the place, time, age, and physical capacity [of the offender].
Having provided food, shelter, fire, water, sacred mantras,
and the expenses for implements to a thief or a murderer who knows [the victim], the highest fine shall be imposed.
In the case of causing an abortion by striking with a weapon, the highest fine is prescribed;
likewise, for the killing of a man or a woman, either the highest or the lowest fine applies.
A woman who has become morally corrupt, one who kills a man, or one who destroys a dam— provided she is not pregnant—
one should cause her to be cast into water after being bound with a stone.
One who administers poison or fire, or one who causes the death of her husband, teacher, or her own child,
should be deprived of life by means of oxen after having had her ears, hands, nose, and lips cut off.

When someone has been killed under circumstances that are not clearly understood, the sons and kinsmen should immediately be questioned, as well as his women who were devoted to other men, each separately.
Or, desiring the woman's property or her means of subsistence, with whom has he departed? Or, one should slowly question people gathered near the place of death.

Those who set fire to fields, houses, forests, villages, pasture lands, or threshing floors, as well as one who has sexual intercourse with the king’s wife, shall be burnt by a straw fire. [End of Chapter 24: Adultery]
In the case of adultery with another's wife, a man should be apprehended by his hair;
or immediately by the signs born of passion, provided there is mutual acknowledgment by both parties.
Touching the waist-knot, the breasts, the upper garment, the thighs, or the hair;
conversing in an improper place or at an improper time; and sitting together on the same seat.
If she refuses, a woman shall pay one hundred [paṇas], but a man shall pay a fine of two hundred;
if both refuse, their punishment shall be the same as in the case of adultery.
In the case of a man of equal caste, the highest fine is prescribed; in the case of a woman of a lower caste (ānulomya), the middle fine;
in the case of a man of a higher caste (prātilomya), death for the male and the cutting off of the ears and so forth for the female.
If one abducts an adorned maiden, he shall pay the highest fine; otherwise, the lowest.
In the case of women of his own caste, he shall pay a fine; however, for abduction in the reverse order of castes, death is ordained by tradition.
There is no offense in approaching women of lower castes who are willing, but otherwise there is punishment;
however, in the case of defilement, the hand shall be cut off, and likewise, death for the highest caste woman.
One should pay one hundred [paṇas] for defiling a woman, but two hundred for making a false accusation;
for approaching cattle, one should be made to pay one hundred, and for approaching a low-caste woman or a cow, the middle amercement.
A man who has sexual intercourse with female slaves who are kept in the household, or likewise with female servants,
even if they are women with whom one may lawfully have relations, shall be made to pay a fine of fifty paṇas.
Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.291ab: (In the case of approaching a female slave by force, a fine of ten paṇas is prescribed.
Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.291cd: If she is unwilling and there are many [men], the fine for each is twenty-four [paṇas].

A prostitute who has accepted her fee shall not, if she is unwilling, be made to pay double; however, if the fee was not accepted, she should be made to pay an equal amount. A man likewise should be treated in exactly the same manner.
For one who approaches a woman in a place other than the vagina, or urinates facing a man,
as well as for one who has sexual intercourse with a female ascetic, the fine is twenty-four [paṇas].
But for approaching a woman of the lowest caste, he should be branded with the mark of a eunuch and banished;

likewise, a Śūdra who approaches a woman of the lowest caste shall be treated as one of the lowest caste himself, while for a man of the highest caste approaching a woman of the lowest caste, the punishment is death.
[25. Section on Miscellaneous Matters]
He who writes a royal edict deficient or even excessive,
or he who releases an adulterer or a thief, shall receive the highest punishment.
One who defiles a twice-born man with forbidden food shall be punished with the highest amercement;
for a Kṣatriya, the middle amercement; for a Vaiśya, the first amercement; and for a Śūdra, half of that.
One who deals in counterfeit gold and one who sells forbidden meat should have three limbs amputated and be made to pay the highest fine.
A fault caused by a four-footed animal does not apply to one who cries out, "Get away!
Likewise, this applies to damage caused by wood, clods of earth, arrows, stones, arms, or draft animals.
If damage is caused by a vehicle whose nose-rope is severed, or whose yoke and other parts are broken,
and which subsequently moves backward, the owner does not incur guilt.

Even if capable of doing so, an owner who does not rescue [a person] from fanged or horned animals shall pay the first *sāhasa* fine; likewise, if [the victim] cries out for help, he shall pay double.
If one addresses a paramour as a "thief," he shall be made to pay a fine of five hundred [paṇas];
if, having lived off his wealth, he abandons him, he shall be made to pay that same amount increased eightfold.
Having cut out the tongue of one who speaks what is undesirable to the king, of one who reviles him, and of one who divulges his counsel, he should banish them.
The punishment for one who sells the limbs of a dead body, for one who strikes his teacher, and likewise for one who mounts the vehicle or seat of the king, is the highest amercement.
For one who pierces two eyes, for one who issues commands hostile to the king,
and likewise for a Śūdra living by means of the status of a Brāhmaṇa, the fine shall be eight hundred.
But if the judges have wrongly decided legal cases,
they, along with the king, shall be fined twice the amount of the dispute.
If one who has been defeated even by legal procedure should think, "I am not defeated," then upon his renewed defeat when he returns, the judge shall cause him to pay double the fine.
The fine that has been unjustly taken by a king, he should personally offer to Varuṇa and give it to the Brahmins multiplied thirtyfold. [End of the Chapter on Legal Procedure]
[III. Chapter on Expiation] [1.
Section on Impurity] Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.1a: One should bury a child less than two years of age; one should not perform the water-libation for them thereafter.
The other [the son], followed by his kinsmen, should follow him as far as the cremation ground.

If he has passed away, he should be cremated with the worldly fire by those reciting the *Yamasūkta* and the *Gāthās*; if he was one who had maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), it should be done according to the ritual procedure for the consecrated fire, as appropriate.
Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.3: Within seven or even ten days, the kinsmen approach [the water] from the direction of the ancestors, saying, "May our sin be burned away by this."
In this same manner, the water-rite (udaka-kriyā) is performed for maternal grandfathers and preceptors who have passed away;
however, the offering of water is optional for friends, married daughters, sisters' sons, fathers-in-law, and officiating priests.

Restraining their speech, they pour water once, pronouncing the name and the lineage; those who are students of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*) shall not perform the water-libation, nor likewise those who are outcasts (*patita*).

Heretics, those who have no refuge, thieves, women who kill their husbands, those who act according to their lust, those who drink liquor, and those who commit suicide— these do not partake in the period of impurity nor in the water libations.
When they have finished the water-rites and emerged, standing upon soft,
grassy ground after their bath, one should address them with ancient historical legends.
He who seeks to find essence in human existence— which is as devoid of substance as the trunk of a plantain tree— is utterly deluded, for it resembles a bubble upon the water.
If this body, composed of five elements, has returned to its fivefold state,
what cause for lamentation is there, since it was brought about by the actions arising from one's own body?
The earth, which supports all beings, shall go to destruction, as will the oceans and the gods;
how then will the mortal world, which resembles mere foam, not perish?
Since the deceased helplessly consumes the phlegm and tears shed by his kinsmen, one should therefore not weep; rather, the funeral rites should be performed according to one's ability.
Having thus made a formal agreement, they should go home preceded by a child;
chewing neem leaves, they should remain restrained at the door of the house.
Having sipped water, they should enter [the house] after touching fire and other [objects], water, cow dung, and white mustard seeds,
and having anointed themselves, they should step slowly upon a stone.
The rites beginning with the entry [into the house] apply even to those who have touched a corpse;
however, for others who desire it, purification occurs instantly through bathing and self-restraint.
Having carried out the funeral rites for his teacher, father, or sub-teacher, one who is under a vow remains a practitioner of that vow;
he should not eat food from a restricted source, nor should he dwell together with them.
Eating food that has been purchased or obtained, they shall sleep separately on the ground; for three days, food should be offered to the deceased according to the ritual procedure of the Piṇḍayajña.
Water and milk should be placed in an earthen vessel for one day in the open air.
The Vaitāna and Aupāsana fires must be maintained, as well as the rites prescribed by the Śruti. Impurity on account of a death is ordained to last either three nights or ten nights.
In the case of a child less than two years old, the period of impurity (sūtaka) for both parents belongs to the mother alone.
Regarding the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) of parents, it is certain that it belongs to the mother because of the manifestation of her blood;
on that day, there is no defilement for the ancestors, because of the cause of their own birth.

In the interval between birth and death, one is purified by the remaining days [of the period of impurity]. In the case of a miscarriage, nights equal in number to the months [of pregnancy] are the cause of purification.
For those killed by kings, cows, or Brahmins, and for those who commit suicide, [the purification occurs] immediately upon sight [of the corpse].
If he has gone abroad, the period remaining shall apply; once that period is completed, he becomes pure by offering water libations.
For a Kṣatriya, the period is twelve days; for a Vaiśya, it is fifteen days;
for a Śūdra, it is thirty days, or half of that (fifteen days) if he lives according to the law.
Until the eruption of teeth, purification is said to be immediate; until the tonsure ceremony (cūḍā), it is one night;
until the initiation into the vows (vratādeśa), it is three nights; and beyond that, it is ten nights.

But for those who have not taken a maiden in marriage, for children, and for the teacher, a pupil, a learned Brahmin (anūcāna), a maternal uncle, and a Śrotriya, the purification lasts one day; as also for sons other than the legitimate son of the body (anaurasa), and for wives who have gone to another man.
When the king who provided residence has died, that very day is the cause of purification.
A Brāhmaṇa must never follow after a Śūdra or another twice-born person. Having followed them, he becomes pure by bathing in water, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter.
There is no period of impurity for lords of the earth when they are killed by lightning,
nor for those who die in battle for the sake of cows or Brahmins, or for whomever the king so desires.

For officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), those who have been consecrated (*dīkṣita*), and those performing sacrificial rites; likewise for those observing the vows of a *sattra* sacrifice, celibate students (*brahmacārin*), donors, and knowers of Brahman.
In giving a gift, in marriage, in a sacrifice, in battle, during a calamity affecting the country,
and even in times of dire distress, immediate purification is prescribed.

If one is touched by a menstruating woman or by impure persons, one should bathe; if touched by them, one should perform ritual sipping of water (*upaspṛśet*). One should also mutter the *ab-liṅga* verses and recite the *Gāyatrī* mantra once mentally.
Time, fire, ritual action, earth, wind, mind, knowledge, austerity, water,
subsequent remorse, and fasting— all these are causes of purification.
For those who have committed forbidden acts, giving gifts, the current of a river, and earth and water for one to be purified,
as well as renunciation, are the means of purification for the twice-born.
Austerity is the strength of those who know the Vedas, patience is the strength of the wise, water is the strength of the body;
for those whose sins are concealed, silent recitation is their strength, and truth is said to be the strength of the mind.
Austerity and knowledge are the purifiers of the elemental self (bhūtātman); wisdom is the purifier of the intellect;
and through the knowledge of the Lord, the purification of the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) is considered supreme. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.34)
A twice-born man may live by the occupation of a Kṣatriya, or even by that of a Vaiśya in times of distress;
having emerged from that distress and having purified himself, he should then settle upon his own proper path.
Fruit, stone, linen, soma, man, cake, and creeper;
sesame, boiled rice, juice, alkali, curd, milk, ghee, and water. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.36)
Weapons, spirituous liquor, honey-remnants, honey, lac, and sacrificial grass;
clay, leather, flowers, blankets, hair, buttermilk, poison, and earth.
Silk, indigo, salt, meat, one-hoofed animals, lead, Śaka, fresh herbs, oil-cakes, and likewise the scents of livestock.
Even while living by the occupation of a Vaiśya, one should never sell sesame seeds; for the sake of dharma, they may be exchanged for an equal amount of grain.
Lac, salt, and meat are causes for falling [from caste] if sold;
however, milk, curd, and liquor cause one to become of a lower caste.
A Brahmin who, having fallen into distress, accepts or consumes food from whatever source may come, is not tainted by sin, for he is equal to fire and the sun.

Agriculture, craftsmanship, service for wages, learning, usury, trade by cart, mountain-mining, service to others, and begging from one's own kin— these are the means of livelihood in times of distress.
If one who is hungry remains for three days, he may take grain from a non-Brāhmaṇa;
having received it, he must report it according to the law when questioned.
Having ascertained his conduct, family, character, learning, Vedic study, austerity, and household, the king shall provide him with a righteous means of livelihood.
[3. The Section on the Duties of the Forest-Dweller] (p.

360) Having entrusted his wife to his son, or accompanied by her, the forest-dweller, remaining celibate, shall go to the forest together with the sacred fires and his ritual implements. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.45)
With produce grown without plowing, the self-possessed man who maintains a beard, matted locks, and body hair should satisfy the fires, the ancestors, the gods, guests, and his dependents.
One should accumulate wealth for a day, a month, six months, or likewise for a year; once it has been accumulated, one should relinquish it in the month of Āśvayuja.
Self-controlled, bathing at the three periods of the day, abstaining from accepting gifts,
devoted to Vedic study, disposed toward giving, and intent on the welfare of all living beings.

He may use his teeth as a mortar, eat only what is ripened by time, or grind his food with a stone; likewise, he should perform the rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, as well as other religious acts, using the juice of fruits and oils.
One should always pass the time with Cāndrāyaṇas or subsist by means of Kṛcchras;
or one may eat when a fortnight has passed, or when a month has passed, or even when a day has passed.

He should sleep on the ground at night, being pure; during the day, he should pass the time by standing on tiptoe, or likewise by alternating between standing, sitting, and walking, or by the practice of yoga.
In the summer, he should stand in the midst of five fires; in the rainy season, he should sleep on the bare ground;
and in the winter, he should wear wet clothes—or he may perform penance according to his capacity.
He who pricks with thorns and he who anoints with sandalwood paste—
toward both of them alike, one should be neither angry nor pleased.
Or, having consigned his sacred fires to himself, dwelling among trees and restricted in food,
he should beg for alms solely for the sake of sustenance from the houses of forest-dwellers.
Or, having brought eight morsels from a village, he should eat them while restraining his speech;
or, subsisting on air, he should walk toward the north-east until his body collapses.
[Chapter 4: The Duties of Ascetics]
Having performed from the forest or from the house a sacrifice in which the entire collection of one's possessions is given as the sacrificial fee (sārvavedasadakṣiṇā),
and having at its conclusion internalized those sacred fires within oneself after performing the Prājāpatya rite;
One who has studied the Vedas, performed silent recitation, fathered sons, given food, maintained the sacred fires,
and offered sacrifices according to his ability— such a person should direct his mind toward liberation, and not otherwise.
Benefiting all beings, peaceful, carrying the triple staff and the water-pot,
dwelling alone in solitude, he should wander forth as a mendicant and enter a village only for the sake of alms.
Vigilant and unobserved, he should go for alms in the evening;
in a village free from other mendicants, he should seek only as much as is necessary for subsistence, without greed.
The vessels of an ascetic are made of clay, bamboo, wood, or gourd;
their purification is by water and scrubbing with cow-hair.
Having restrained the collection of the senses, having abandoned passion and hatred,
and having cast off fear toward all beings, the twice-born man becomes immortal.
A mendicant, however, must especially purify his inner disposition,
because it is the cause for the arising of knowledge and for the attainment of independence.
One should contemplate the dwellings in the womb and the various states of existence born of karma,
as well as mental anxieties, physical diseases, afflictions, old age, and the transformation of one's physical form.
The reversal of the pleasant and unpleasant occurs throughout thousands of births;
one who is established as a subtle self within the self should perceive this through the yoga of meditation.
Indeed, the stage of life (*āśrama*) is not the cause of *dharma*; rather, it becomes so when [the duty] is being performed.
Therefore, one should not do that which is unwholesome for oneself to others.
Truthfulness, non-stealing, freedom from anger, modesty, purity, wisdom, fortitude, self-restraint,
control of the senses, and learning— these are declared to be the entirety of dharma.
"Just as sparks issue forth from a heated mass of iron,
even so do individual selves indeed emerge from the Self."
In that regard, the self indeed performs some action by itself, some through its own nature, and some—
consisting of both merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*)— through habitual practice.
The cause, the imperishable, the agent, the knower, the possessor of qualities,
and the controller— though unborn, it is proclaimed to be "born" due to the assumption of a body.
Just as at the beginning of creation he emits space, wind, light, water, and earth—
each possessing one additional quality— so too, while coming into being, he takes them up again.
Through the oblation the sun is nourished; from the sun comes rain, and then the plants.
That food, in the form of sap, attains the state of semen.
But when there is union between a woman and a man, and the semen and blood are pure,
the Lord himself, as the sixth, simultaneously takes up the five elements.
The sense organs, the mind, the vital breath, knowledge, life-span, happiness, fortitude, retention, impulse, suffering, desire, and indeed the ego-sense; (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.73).
Effort, form, color, accentuation, aversion, existence, and non-existence—
all this is born of that [Self] as it desires a beginning for itself, though it is without beginning.
In the first month, it becomes a mass of moisture, coagulated with the bodily constituents;
in the second month, it becomes an *arbuda*; and in the third month, it is endowed with limbs and sense organs.
From ether [come] lightness, subtlety, sound, the sense of hearing, strength, and so forth;
and from air [come] the sense of touch, movement, expansion, and dryness.
From bile (pitta) arise vision, digestion, heat, color, and luminosity;
from phlegm (rasa), however, arise taste, coldness, unctuousness, moisture, and softness.
In the third [state], the immutable Self grasps the smell of the earth, as well as the sense of smell, heaviness, and even form; thereafter, it vibrates.
By failing to grant her pregnancy-longing, the fetus may incur deformity or even death; therefore, one should fulfill what is dear to the woman.
In the fourth month, there is stability of the limbs; in the fifth, the emergence of blood;
and in the sixth, the development of strength, complexion, nails, and hair.
In the seventh and eighth [weeks], he is endowed with consciousness and mind, possessed of channels, sinews, and veins, and also possesses skin, flesh, and memory.
Again the *dhātrī* (nurse), again the *gharma* (heat)—his vital energy (*ojas*) flows away from him. Consequently, the fetus born in the eighth month is deprived of its life-breaths (*prāṇa*).
In the ninth or even the tenth month, by powerful birth-winds,
he is expelled like an arrow through the opening of a machine, accompanied by feverish pain.
Its bodies are sixfold, and it possesses six layers of skin;
likewise, its limbs are six, and its bones amount to three hundred and sixty.
Together with the sockets, there are sixty-four teeth; the nails are twenty;
and the bones of the hands and feet constitute their four locations.
There are sixty finger-breadths (aṅgulis) in the two heels; four in the ankles;
four bones in the forearms (aratnis); and exactly as many in the two shanks (jaṅghās).
One should point out that there are two each produced from the knees, the cheeks, the thighs, the shoulder-blades,
the eyes, the palate, the uvula, and the pelvic bones.
The hip consists of one bone; likewise, there are forty-five bones in the back.
The neck consists of fifteen bones; each clavicle is a single bone, as is the jaw.
At the base of those [joints] are two: the forehead-eye and the cheek; the nose consists of compact bone;
the ribs together with the sockets and the arbudas are seventy-two.
There are two temples (śaṅkhaka), four skull-bones (kapāla), and likewise seventeen bones for the chest; such is the collection of bones in a human being.
Smell, form, taste, touch, and sound are recorded as the objects of the senses;
the nose, eyes, tongue, skin, and ears are the sense organs.
One should know that the hands, the anus, the generative organ, the tongue, and the feet are indeed the five organs of action; and the mind is of the nature of both.
The navel, the vital energy (ojas), the anus, the semen, the blood, as well as the two temples,
the head, the shoulders, the throat, and the heart— these are the seats of the vital breath (prāṇa).
The omentum, the fat, the slaughter-wound, the navel, the lungs, the liver, the spleen;
the small intestine, the kidneys, the bladder, and the receptacle of excrement;
the stomach, the heart, the large intestine, and the rectum.
The abdomen and the two pelvic cavities—this is declared to be the width.
The two pupils, the two eye-sockets, the two ear-cavities, the two ear-flaps,
the two ears, the two temples, the two eyebrows, the two gums, the two lips, and the two hollows of the loins.
The groins, the testicles, the kidneys, and the breasts are produced from the accumulation of phlegm;
likewise are the uvula, the buttocks, the arms, and the muscles of the calves and thighs.
The palate, the stomach, the top of the bladder, the chin, the two tonsils, and the navel—
these are the locations in this body.
The two eyes, the two ears, the two feet, the hands, and the heart—
these nine apertures are indeed the abodes of the vital breath (prāṇa).
There are exactly seven hundred channels (śirā), nine hundred ligaments (snāyu),
two hundred vessels (dhamanī), and five hundred muscles (peśī).
Know that there are twenty-nine lakhs,
nine hundred and fifty-six vessels known as *dhamanīs*.
It should be known that there are three hundred thousand hairs on the body, including the beard and head hair;
likewise, there are one hundred and seven vital points (*marmans*) and two hundred joints.
There are fifty-four crores,
sixty-seven lakhs, and fifty thousand pores of the hair, together with the openings of the sweat-glands.
Even if one were to comprehend their nature and their very arrangement, the individual atoms are reckoned as being composed of aerial particles once they have been divided.
Nine añjalis of liquid are to be known [as the measure], and ten añjalis for water;
seven indeed for feces, and eight are proclaimed for blood.
Phlegm is six [parts], bile five, and urine four;
muscle-fat three, fat two, marrow one, and half [a part] is in the head.
"The phlegm has such-and-such strength, the vital energy has such-and-such strength, and the semen likewise has such-and-such strength"—
he who possesses this unstable body should strive for liberation.
Seventy-two thousand channels (nāḍīs) issue forth from the heart; among them is one named Hitā, shining with the luster of the moon.
The self situated in the center of that orb is motionless like a lamp.
That is to be known; having realized it here, one is not born again.
And that Āraṇyaka which I obtained from the Sun should be known; likewise, the Yoga-śāstra proclaimed by me should be studied by one who desires to attain Yoga.
Having made the mind, intellect, memory, and senses focused on no other object,
the Self— who resides here in the heart like a lamp as the sovereign Lord— should be meditated upon.
By reciting the Sāman chants according to the prescribed rules, without error and with focused attention,
one attains the supreme Brahman through such practice.
The *ullopya*, *madraka*, *prakarī*, *apara-antaka*, *auveṇaka*, *saro-bindu*, and the *uttara* songs; these are the types of singing. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.113)
The *ṛk-gāthā*, the *pāṇikā*, the *dakṣavihitā*, and the *brahmagītikā*—this is what is to be sung; through the practice of it, it is designated as "liberation."
One who knows the true principles of playing the lute, is proficient in the *śrutis* and *jātis*,
and understands the rhythmic measures (*tāla*), attains the path to liberation without effort.
If one who knows song does not attain the supreme state through yoga,
he becomes an attendant of Rudra and rejoices together with him.
The self is said to be beginningless, but its beginning is the body;
the entire universe originates from the self, and the self arises from the universe.
"How is this world—including gods, asuras, and humans—produced? And how is the Self [involved] therein? Tell us this, for we are bewildered."
Indeed, that person who is seen here after casting off the net of delusion possesses a thousand hands,
feet, and eyes, and has a thousand forms with the brilliance of the sun.
He is the Self, the sacrifice, and Prajāpati of universal form;
as Virāj, he attains the state of sacrifice through the form of food.
That supreme essence which arises from the renunciation of substances and deities,
having fully satisfied the gods, [satisfies] the sacrificer with its fruit.
Having joined the Soma with the wind, it is then led upward by the rays;
having been brought to the solar abode ordained by the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman, it is conveyed there.
From the orb of the sky, that Sun emits the supreme nectar,
from which all beings— whether they subsist on food or do not eat— take their birth.
From that food, again comes sacrifice; from sacrifice, again food; and from food, again sacrifice. Thus does this wheel revolve, without beginning or end.
The self is beginningless; there is no origination of the inner self. However, the person (puruṣa) is a composite entity born of delusion, desire, aversion, and karma.
"He who was proclaimed by me as the primordial god, whose self is a thousandfold— for him,
the social classes (varṇas) arose from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet, respectively."
From his feet the earth was born; from his head the sky arose;
from his nose the vital breaths, from his ears the directions, from his touch the wind, and from his mouth the fire.
From his mind the moon was born, and from his eye the sun;
from his loins arose the intermediate space and the world of moving and unmoving beings.
If this is so, O Brahmin, how is it that he is born into sinful wombs?
How does that Lord become joined with undesirable states of being?
And how is it that there was no prior knowledge [of the soul] even though it was endowed with the instruments [of perception]?
Why does the omnipresent [soul], though itself omnipresent, not perceive the sensation [experienced by another]?
Through defects born of actions of mind, speech, and body, this living soul attains the state of lower animals, birds, and immobile beings, and undergoes existence within hundreds of wombs.
Just as the states of embodied beings within their bodies are infinite,
so too are the forms of those possessing bodies here in all wombs.
The ripening of some actions occurs after death, while for others it arises in this world;
for yet others, it occurs both here and there—the state of being [in these realms] is the purpose of that [karma].
Coveting the property of others, likewise brooding over what is undesirable,
and being intent upon falsehoods, one is born into other wombs.
A man who speaks falsehoods, a slanderer, one who speaks harshly,
and one who engages in incoherent prattle is born among wild animals and birds.
One who delights in taking what is not given, one who courts the wives of others,
and one who causes injury to stationary beings in a manner contrary to the rules, is born among stationary things.
One who knows the self, is pure, self-controlled, ascetic, has conquered his senses, performs dharma, and is learned in Vedic knowledge— such a person of sattvic nature attains the state of a deity.
He who delights in improper actions, is undisciplined, impulsive, and addicted to sensual objects— he,
being of the *rājasa* nature among men, attains birth after death.
One who is prone to sleep, cruel, greedy, an atheist, a beggar,
as well as one who is negligent and of broken conduct, becomes a tamasic being among the animals.
Thus, possessed by both passion and darkness, wandering here in this world and joined with undesirable states of being, he enters the cycle of transmigration.
For just as a dirty mirror is incapable of reflecting a form,
so too a person whose faculties are undigested is incapable of self-knowledge.

Just as in an unripe mango, even though the sweet taste is present within, it cannot be perceived; so too, when the instruments [of cognition] are unrefined, the state of being a knower is not realized within the self.
The embodied soul experiences all sensations based upon its own body;
yet the yogin who is liberated does not experience any of those sensations.
Just as the single ether appears distinct within jars and other vessels,
so too the one Self appears as many, like the sun reflected in various receptacles of water.
Brahman, ether, air, fire, water, and earth are the primary elements;
from these [arise] these worlds, this self, and everything moving and unmoving.

Just as a potter makes a jar from the conjunction of clay, a staff, and a wheel, or as a house-builder constructs a house with grass, earth, and wood; [so does the agent produce an effect through the conjunction of various causes].

Just as a goldsmith, taking only a small amount of gold or a piece of base metal, produces a vessel through the addition of his own saliva; or just as a silkworm produces a cocoon [from its own secretions].
Having thus taken up the instruments [of action], the Self, having come together with those various instruments, creates itself within those various wombs in this world.
The great elements are real, and the self is likewise so;
for who, having seen with one eye, sees with the other otherwise?
Who indeed understands speech once it has been heard again after being heard?
To whom belongs the memory of a past object, and who is the creator of a dream?
One who is conceited on account of birth, appearance, age, conduct, learning, and so forth,
exerts himself toward the objects of the senses— sound and the rest— through action, mind, and speech.
With his mind clouded by doubt as to whether the fruit of action exists or not, he is deluded;
for even though he has not attained perfection, he considers himself to have attained it.
"My wife, son, and ministers; I am theirs"—such is his fixed notion.
He always possesses a perverted mind regarding matters that are beneficial or harmful.

One who makes no distinction between the object of knowledge and the knower, or between the primordial nature (prakṛti) and its transformations (vikāra), and one who attempts suicide by fasting, fire, weapons, water, or by throwing oneself down from a precipice; [these are excluded from the rites].
One who behaves in this manner, whose self is undisciplined, and who possesses false attachments,
is bound by his actions through hatred, delusion, and desire.
Service to the teacher, discernment regarding the meanings of the Vedas and the Shastras,
the performance of those prescribed duties, association with the virtuous, and auspicious speech.
Avoiding the sight of women and their touch, perceiving the self in all beings,
renouncing possessions, and wearing a worn-out saffron robe.
Restraining the senses from their objects, abandoning drowsiness and laziness,
keeping close watch over the body, and perceiving the evil in worldly activities.
Purity of *sattva* consists in being free from *rajas* and *tamas*, as well as desirelessness and tranquility.
Purified by these means, one who is fit for *sattva* becomes immortal.

Through the recollection of reality, through the presence [of the mind], through the union with *sattva*, through the complete exhaustion of karmas, and through proximity to the virtuous, the yoga of the good proceeds.
He whose mind, at the dissolution of the body, is established in the Lord and grounded in *sattva*,
with his intellect unconfused, shall truly attain the recollection of his former births.
Just as Bharata colors his own body with pigments,
assuming various forms, so too does the Self assume bodies born of karma.
The deformity of the embryo at birth—such as being deficient in limbs—is seen to result from defects in time, karma, the self, and the seed, as well as those of the mother. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.163)
