This self has never before been liberated from egoism, the mind, the sense of motion, the fruit of action, and the body in any way whatsoever.
Just as the continued existence of a lamp depends on the combination of the wick, the vessel,
and the oil, so too is the premature destruction of life observed to occur despite such [causes].
Infinite are his rays, situated in the heart like a lamp—
white, black, variegated, tawny, blue, and red.
Among them, he who stands alone above, having pierced the solar orb and transcended the world of Brahmā, goes by that path to the supreme goal.
That other hundred rays of his which are situated upwards— by means of them,
he attains the celestial bodies together with their abodes.
And those rays of his which are of many forms below and possess a mild luster—
with them he wanders helplessly in this world for the sake of experiencing the fruits of his actions.
By means of the Vedas, the Śāstras, and specialized knowledge; by birth and by death;
likewise by suffering, by going, and by not going; indeed, by truth and by falsehood.
Through better or worse happiness and suffering, through auspicious and inauspicious actions,
and through the fruits arising from omens, the knowledge of birds, and the conjunctions of the planets.
Through the movements of the stars and constellations, through wakefulness and even those born of sleep, as well as through space, wind, light, water, earth, and darkness; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.172.
Through the Manvantaras, through the attainment of the Yugas, and even through mantras, medicinal herbs, and fruits—
one should know oneself as the cause of the world, which is thus perceived.
Egoism, memory, intelligence, aversion, intellect, pleasure, fortitude, the transition between the senses, desire, retention, and life—these [are the functions of the mind]. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.174)
Heaven, dreaming, the impelling of entities, the movement of the mind,
the winking of an eye, consciousness, effort, and grasping— all these consist of the five elements.
Since these marks of the supreme self are observed,
therefore there exists a self beyond the body, all-pervading and sovereign.

The sense organs together with their objects, the mind, the organs of action, as well as the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), the intellect (buddhi), and the elements beginning with earth; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.177.

The unmanifest Self is declared to be the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) of this field; it is the Lord dwelling within all beings, who is both being and non-being, and both existent and non-existent.
The emergence of the intellect (buddhi) occurs from the unmanifest (avyakta); from that, the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) arises.
From the ego-sense, the subtle elements (tanmātra) and the rest arise, each possessing one additional quality [than its predecessor].
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are their qualities;
whichever among these has emerged from which [element], that dissolves back into that very same one.
Just as the Self creates itself, so has it been described by me to you;
although He is the Lord, He does so through the ripening of the three kinds of karmas.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are indeed proclaimed to be its very qualities;
for when possessed by rajas and tamas, it revolves like a wheel.
He alone is the supreme Puruṣa, both without beginning and yet possessing a beginning;
he is declared to be subject to transformation, with a form perceivable by the subtle and gross senses.
By that path which lies between the Pitṛyāna, the Ajavīthī, and Agastya,
those who maintain the sacred fire and desire heaven proceed toward the celestial realm.
And those who are devoted to giving, properly endowed with the eight qualities,
and dedicated to the vow of truth— they too proceed by that very same path.
Among them, eighty-eight thousand sages were householders;
they were subject to rebirth, served as the seed [of future lineages], and were the propagators of dharma.
Residing in the celestial world within the paths of the Seven Sages and the Nāgas,
there are just as many sages who have abandoned all undertakings.
By means of austerity, celibacy, renunciation of attachment, and wisdom,
they go there and remain until the dissolution of all beings.
From which [the Vedas] come— the Purāṇas, the Vidyās, and the Upaniṣads,
as well as the Ślokas, Sūtras, Bhāṣyas, and whatever else consists of speech.
The recitation of the Veda, sacrifice, celibacy, austerity, self-restraint,
faith, fasting, and independence are the causes for the knowledge of the Self.
For he is indeed to be sought after by all the stages of life in this very manner;
thus he is to be seen, reflected upon, and heard by the twice-born.
Those twice-born who, having resorted to the forest, know this [truth] thus, and worship it with supreme faith, attain the Truth.
In due order, they arise as the flame, the day, the bright fortnight, the northern solstice,
the world of the gods, the sun, and the lightning.
Then a person born of the mind, having approached them, makes them inhabitants of the world of Brahman;
for them, there is no returning here again.
For those men who have conquered heaven through sacrifice, austerity, and gifts,
[they travel] through smoke, the night, the dark fortnight, and the southern solstice.
The world of the ancestors, the moon, the wind, rain, water, and the earth—
they reach these in succession here, and from there they return once again.
That self-possessed man who does not understand these two paths shall become either a venomous serpent, a moth, an insect, or a worm.

With his feet placed on his thighs and turned upward, having placed his left hand upon his right which is also turned upward, and slightly lifting his face while supporting it with his chest; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.198.
With eyes closed, established in the quality of goodness (*sattva*), not letting the teeth touch the teeth,
with the tongue motionless against the palate, the mouth closed, and perfectly still.
Having restrained the collection of the senses and sitting on a seat that is neither too low nor too high,
one should undertake breath-control (prāṇāyāma) either twice or thrice.
Then the wise man, maintaining his concentration (*dhāraṇā*), should fix his self upon that Lord who resides in the heart like a lamp and is to be meditated upon.
Invisibility, the power of recollection, radiance, the faculty of sight, as well as the faculty of hearing,
and likewise the ability to enter the bodies of others after casting off one's own body.
The creation of objects at will is indeed the mark of perfection in yoga;
for one who has perfected yoga, by casting off the body, he is fit for immortality.
Alternatively, even one who has renounced ritual acts and dwells in the forest, reciting the Veda,
eating moderately and subsisting on what is unasked for, shall attain the highest perfection.

One who has acquired wealth by righteous means, who is devoted to the knowledge of reality, who is fond of guests, who performs ancestral rites, and who speaks the truth— even such a householder is indeed liberated. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.205)
Having reached the terrible and dreadful hells born of great sins,
those who have committed great sins are reborn here upon the exhaustion of their karma.
The killer of a Brahmin enters the womb of a deer, a horse, a boar, or a camel;
the drinker of liquor [enters] the womb of a donkey, a Pulkasa, or a Vena—of this there is no doubt.
A thief of gold shall become a worm, an insect, or a winged insect; and one who violates the teacher’s bed shall gradually become a grass, a shrub, or a creeper.

A killer of a Brahmin shall suffer from a wasting disease; a drinker of spirituous liquor, from black teeth; a stealer of gold, from deformed nails; and one who violates the teacher’s bed, from skin disease. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.209)
Whichever of these one associates with, one is born bearing the characteristics of that person:
a stealer of food shall suffer from indigestion, and a stealer of speech shall be mute.
One who mixes grain [with inferior quality] shall have an extra limb; a slanderer, a putrid nose;
one who steals oil shall be an oil-drinker; and a backbiter, a foul-mouthed person.
Having abducted another’s wife and having stolen the property of a Brahmin,
one becomes a Brahma-rākṣasa in a waterless region in the forest.
One who steals the precious jewels of another is born into a low caste; by killing a peacock one becomes a parrot, and by stealing fine perfumes one becomes a muskrat.

A mouse shall be the thief of grain; a camel the thief of a vehicle; a monkey the thief of fruit; a water-fowl the thief of water; a crow the thief of milk; and a house-builder bird the thief of household utensils.
A gadfly [destroys] honey, a vulture a piece of meat, a monitor lizard a cow, and a crane likewise fire;
a leper [destroys] clothing, a dog a savory juice, and a cricket one who steals salt.
This has been stated by me for the purpose of illustration regarding the act of theft;
for the varieties of objects are indeed just like the classes of living beings.
Having obtained the fruit of their actions according to their deeds, through the passage of time, they are born as animals;
then, fallen from auspicious marks, they become poor and the lowest of men.
Then, having become free from taint, they are born into a great family as enjoyers of life's pleasures,
endowed with knowledge and possessed of wealth and grain.
By the non-performance of what is prescribed, by the practice of what is censured,
and by the lack of restraint over the senses, a man undergoes a fall.
Therefore, he must perform an expiation here for the sake of purification;
in this way, both his inner self and the world become propitiated.
Men who are devoted to sins and do not perform penance, being free from remorse,
go to terrible and dreadful hells.
Tāmisra, Lohaśaṅku, Mahāniraya, Śālmalī, Raurava, Kuḍmala, Pūtimṛttika, and Kālasūtraka.
Saṃghāta, Lohitoda, Saviṣa, Saṃprapātana,
Mahānarakakākola, Saṃjīvana, and Mahāpatha.
Avīci, Andhatāmisra, and likewise Kumbhīpāka; Asipatravana and Tāpana—these constitute the twenty-first [hell].

Those lowest of men who have not performed expiation remain afflicted by the terrible sins arising from mortal transgressions (*mahāpātaka*) as well as those arising from minor transgressions (*upapātaka*).

Sins committed through ignorance may be removed by expiatory rites; however, one who acts intentionally becomes subject to legal proceedings here [in this world] according to the scriptural injunctions.

The killer of a Brahmin, a drinker of intoxicants, a thief, and likewise one who violates the teacher’s bed— these are the perpetrators of mortal sins (mahāpātakin), as is anyone who associates with them.

Excessive abuse of one's gurus, reviling the Vedas, the killing of a friend, and the destruction of what has been studied—these should be known as equal to the murder of a Brahmin. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.228)
Eating forbidden food, deceitfulness, speaking falsehood for the sake of self-exaltation,
and tasting the mouth of a woman in her menses are equal to the drinking of liquor.
The seizure of a horse, a gem, a human being, a woman, land, or a milch cow,
as well as that of a deposit, is indeed equal to the theft of gold.

Sexual intercourse with the wife of a friend, with virgins, with women of one's own womb (uterine sisters), with women of the lowest castes, with women of the same lineage (gotra), or with women closely related by marriage is declared to be equal to violating the teacher’s bed.
The father’s sister, the mother’s sister, the maternal uncle’s wife, and even a daughter-in-law;
likewise, the mother’s co-wife, a sister, and the teacher’s daughter.
He who approaches the wife of his teacher or his own daughter is a violator of the Guru's bed; his penis shall be cut off and he shall be executed, as shall the woman if she was willing.
Killing a cow, being a *vrātya*, theft, non-payment of debts, failing to maintain the sacred fires, selling goods that should not be sold, and gambling; (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.234).
Receiving instruction for a fee, teaching for a fee, adultery, marrying a woman already married, usury, and the manufacture of salt; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.235.
The killing of a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya; living by means of reprehensible wealth; atheism; the neglect of religious vows; and the sale of one's own sons.

The theft of grain, base metals, or livestock; officiating at sacrifices for those for whom one should not sacrifice; the abandonment of one's father, mother, or son; and the sale of a tank or a grove.

Defiling a maiden, officiating at the marriage of one who has already married his younger sister before the elder, giving a daughter in marriage to such a person, dishonesty, and the violation of a vow; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.238.

Undertaking ritual actions for one's own sake, consorting with women who drink liquor, abandoning the study of the Vedas, the sacred fires, and one's children, as well as the abandonment of kinsmen; Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.239.
Cutting down trees for the sake of fuel, harming women, living by the sale of medicinal herbs, constructing lethal traps, and the sale of oneself— these are vices.
Service to a Śūdra, friendship with the low-born, consorting with those of inferior birth,
likewise dwelling outside the stages of life (āśramas), and being nourished by the food of others.
Studying false scriptures, engaging in mining operations,
and the sale of one's wife— each of these is a minor offense (upapātaka).
Carrying a skull as his banner, subsisting on alms while proclaiming his deed,
the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa shall attain purification by eating sparingly for twelve years.
By rescuing a Brāhmaṇa or twelve cows,
or likewise by bathing at the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), one attains purification.
Having seen on the road a Brāhmaṇa or even a cow afflicted by a long-standing or severe illness, the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa becomes pure by setting them free from danger.
Having recovered the entire property of a Brāhmaṇa that was stolen, or having caused its thief to be slain,
or even while still alive, one who has been wounded by weapons on account of that act is purified.
With the words "Svāhā to the body hairs," he should indeed offer the body starting from the hair down to the marrow, using these mantras in their proper sequence.
Or, having become a target in battle, he may attain purification when slain;
even if still living, he is purified if he is nearly dead, afflicted by a mortal wound.
Or, being self-restrained, having recited the Saṃhitā of the Veda three times in the forest,
he may be purified by eating measured food while following the Sarasvatī river against its current.
Or, by giving a sufficient amount of wealth to a worthy recipient, one attains purification;
and for the sake of the donor's purification, the Vaiśvānara sacrifice is prescribed by tradition.

One who kills a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya engaged in a sacrifice shall perform the vow prescribed for a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa; likewise one who destroys a fetus according to its caste, as well as one who kills an Ātreyī woman.

One should perform the penance even if one has not killed [the victim], provided one approached with the intent to kill; however, if the Brāhmaṇa was engaged in a Soma sacrifice, one should prescribe double the penance.
Having drunk any one of these— liquor, water, clarified butter, cow urine, or milk— that has become like fire,
the drinker of liquor attains purification through death.
Clad in animal hair or wearing matted locks, he shall perform the vow for the murder of a Brahmin;
or he may eat oil-cake or grain-husks at night for three years.
But having unintentionally drunk *surā*, or [consumed] semen, feces,
or urine, the three twice-born castes deserve to undergo the rite of re-initiation (*punaḥsaṃskāra*).
That Brāhmaṇī woman who drinks liquor does not go to the world of her husband;
in this very world, she is reborn as a female dog, a vulture, and a sow.
But the stealer of a Brāhmaṇa’s gold shall offer a mace to the king;
having confessed his own deed, he is purified whether he is killed by it or released.
Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.258: Without reporting [the offense] to the king, one who performs the penance for drinking liquor shall become purified;
or he may give gold equal to his own weight, or do what brings satisfaction to a Brahmin.
On a bed of heated iron, he shall lie with an iron image of a woman;
having seized and cut off his testicles, he shall cast away his body toward the region of Nirṛti.
One who has violated the Guru’s bed shall perform the Prājāpatya penance for one year,
or he shall recite the Vedic Saṃhitā for three months while observing the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
But he who associates with these for a year becomes equal to them;
he may marry a maiden from among them who is fasting and possesses no property.
Having killed any of those who are outcastes, however, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Even a Śūdra, though deprived of the right [to perform Vedic rites], becomes pure through this same period of time.
The killer of a cow shall drink the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) for one month, remaining self-controlled;
sleeping in a cow-pen and following after the cows, he is purified by the gift of a cow.
Or, being composed in mind, he should perform the Kṛcchra and the Atikṛcchra penances;
or, having fasted for three nights, he should give away cows with a bull as the eleventh.
Purification for minor offenses (upapātaka) may be achieved in this manner by means of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance,
or else by subsisting on milk for a month, or again by the Parāka penance.
For killing a Kṣatriya, a man should give one thousand cows with a bull as the eleventh,
or he should observe the vow for the murder of a Brāhmaṇa for three years.
A killer of a Vaiśya shall perform this penance for one year, or else give one hundred and one cows;
a killer of a Śūdra shall perform this for six months, or else give ten cows.
Having caused the death of women of the Brāhmaṇa, Vaiśya, Kṣatriya, or Śūdra castes who have behaved wickedly,
one should give, respectively, a leather water-bag, a bow, a goat, or a sheep for the sake of purification.
Having killed a woman who has not committed a heinous crime, one should perform the penance prescribed for killing a Śūdra;
likewise, for killing a thousand vertebrate animals, or an equal number of invertebrates.
Having killed a cat, an iguana, a mongoose, a frog, or birds,
one should drink milk for three days or perform the *kṛcchra* penance consisting of a quarter-portion (*pādika*).
For an elephant, five dark-blue bulls; for a parrot, a two-year-old calf;
for donkeys, goats, and rams, a bull; and for a crane, a three-year-old bull should be given.
Having killed a swan, a hawk, a monkey, a carnivorous animal, a water-fowl, a land-fowl, or a peacock, one should give a cow; but having killed a non-carnivorous bird, one should give a heifer.
For [stealing] snakes, an iron rod [shall be given]; for a eunuch, tin and lead; for a boar, a jar of ghee; for a camel, a *guñjā* seed; and for a horse, a fine silk garment.

If one is unable to give a drona of sesame seeds for each of the offenses beginning with the killing of an elephant, one should perform a *kṛcchra* penance for the purification of each individual offense. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.274)

Upon killing a living being produced from fruit, flower, food, or sap, one must consume clarified butter (*ghṛta*). For the killing of something with bones, something small should be given; however, for that which is boneless, one should perform a breath-control exercise (*prāṇāyāma*). For cutting trees, shrubs, creepers, or climbing plants, one hundred *ṛc* verses are to be recited.
For the useless cutting of medicinal herbs, one should follow a cow for a day while subsisting on milk.
One who has been bitten by a promiscuous woman, a monkey, a donkey, a dog, a camel, or the like, or by a crow,
becomes purified by performing breath-control (prāṇāyāma) in water and consuming clarified butter (ghṛta).
With the two verses beginning "That semen of mine today," he should consecrate the spilled semen;
with that [semen], he should touch the space between the breasts and the middle of the eyebrows using the ring finger.
Having seen one's own reflection in water, one should mutter "May splendor be in me";
likewise, when seeing something impure, or when there is restlessness, or even in the case of falsehood, one should mutter the Sāvitrī.
A religious student who, having gone to a woman, becomes an *avakīrṇin*,
is purified by sacrificing a donkey as an animal dedicated to Nirṛti.
Having neglected the alms-gathering and the fire-ritual for seven nights while not being ill,
one who has emitted semen intentionally should offer two oblations with these two [verses].
Then one should perform the propitiation with this [mantra]: "May they sprinkle me together. For eating honey or meat, a *kṛcchra* penance and the remaining vows must be performed.
Having acted in opposition to his guru, one becomes purified only after propitiating him;
if the guru dies while being sent on a mission, the offender should perform three *kṛcchra* penances. However, if a Brahmin dies while receiving assistance, there is no sin.
In the case of the digestion of bulls, or in the administration of medicine and fire-rituals,
the guilt of one who makes a false accusation is double that of one who speaks the truth.
He who speaks falsely incurs the guilt of one who has been falsely accused;
he who falsely charges another with a major or minor sin shall fast on water for a month, reciting prayers with his senses restrained.
One who has been falsely accused should perform the Kṛcchra penance or the Āgneya penance;
alternatively, he should offer a Puroḍāśa cake to Vāyu or even a sacrificial animal to Vāyu.
One who, being unappointed, approaches his brother's wife, shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
having approached a woman in her courses, he becomes pure after consuming clarified butter at the end of three nights.
One who officiates for a Vrātya, even if performing malevolent magic, shall perform three Kṛcchra penances;
likewise one who has forgotten the Veda, having subsisted on barley for a year, and one who has abandoned someone who has come for refuge.
A student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) who dwells for one month in a cow-pen,
subsisting on milk and devoted to the recitation of the *Gāyatrī*, is purified from the acceptance of improper gifts.
Having bathed in water while practicing breath-restraint, one is purified from riding a donkey or a camel;
likewise, having bathed naked, or having eaten [while naked], or having gone to a woman by day, one is purified in the same way.
Having addressed a guru as "thou," or having defeated a Brahmin in debate,
or having bound him with a garment, one must quickly appease him and fast for a day.
For raising a staff against a Brahmin, one must perform the Kṛcchra penance; for striking him down, the Atikṛcchra;
for shedding blood, the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra; and for internal bleeding, the Kṛcchra.
Having carefully considered the place, the time, the age, the capacity, and the nature of the offense,
an expiation should be prescribed where no specific atonement has been stated.
The kinsmen of the outcast should carry a pitcher of water outside the village;
they should exclude him from all social functions.
When he has completed his vow and returned, they should pour out water from a new jar; they should not despise him, nor should they live with him in any way whatsoever.
This same rule for those who have fallen from their caste is proclaimed for women as well:
they should be given clothing at the edge of the house, along with food and protection.
Approaching a man of low caste, causing an abortion, and harming her husband—
these also are certainly specific causes of loss of caste for women.
One should not dwell with those who harm one who has come for refuge, children, or women—even if they have performed their penances—nor with these: the ungrateful and their associates.
When the water-jar has been set aside, he who stands among his kinsmen should provide fodder for the cows;
for this is the first act of hospitality shown to one who has been honored by the cows.
One whose offense is publicly known should perform a vow approved by an assembly;
however, one whose offense is not publicly known should perform a secret vow.
Having fasted for three nights and recited the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn while submerged in water, a killer of a Brahmin is purified by giving a milch cow.
Or, subsisting on air for a day, he should offer forty oblations of clarified butter while standing in water, reciting: "Svāhā to the body hairs! (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.302).
Having fasted for three nights and offered clarified butter with the *kūṣmāṇḍī* verses, one becomes pure;
but a stealer of a Brāhmaṇa’s gold, remaining in water while reciting the *rudra* hymns, is purified.
One who has violated the Guru’s bed is liberated by reciting the *sahasra-śīrṣā* [hymn].
At the conclusion of this rite, a milch cow should be given by each of these separately.
One hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) should be performed for the removal of all sins,
as well as for the various minor offenses (upapātakas) and those for which no specific penance has been prescribed.
Having consumed semen, feces, or urine, the best of the twice-born should drink purifying water consecrated with the syllable *oṃ*. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.306)
Whatever has been done through ignorance, whether by night or even by day,
all that perishes by performing the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) at the three times of day.
The recitation of the Śukriya and Āraṇyaka texts, and especially that of the Gāyatrī—
these, as well as the Rudra-ekādaśinī, are indeed removers of all sins.
Wherever a twice-born man perceives himself to be defiled,
there he should perform an oblation with sesame seeds and likewise recite the Gāyatrī mantra.

Sinful acts, even those arising from the great crimes (*mahāpātaka*), do not touch one who is devoted to the study of the Vedas, who is patient, and who is intent on the performance of the five sacrifices.
Subsisting on air, standing during the day and spending the night in water while gazing at the sun,
and having recited the Gāyatrī a thousand times, one is purified— except for the killing of a Brāhmaṇa.
Celibacy, compassion, forbearance, charity, truthfulness, sincerity,
non-violence, abstention from theft, gentleness, and self-control— these are declared in the Smṛti to be the *yamas*.
Bathing, silence, fasting, sacrifice, Vedic study, restraint of the generative organ,
service to the teacher, purity, freedom from anger, and vigilance are the observances (niyamas).
Having consumed cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass,
one should fast on the following day and perform the *sāntapana-kṛcchra* penance.
For six days, one should consume the substances of the Sāntapana penance separately and observe a fast on the seventh day;
this seven-day rite is known as the Mahāsāntapana Kṛcchra.
When the leaves of the *parṇa*, *udumbara*, *rājīva*, and *bilva* trees, along with *kuśa* grass and water,
are drunk individually every day, it is declared to be the *parṇakṛcchra*.
One should drink each of these—boiled milk, ghee, and water—daily for one day;
this, along with fasting for one night, is declared to be the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
Eating once a day, eating only at night, likewise eating only what is unasked for,
and fasting— this is proclaimed as the Pādakṛcchra penance.
In whatever manner it may be performed, this threefold [fast] is called the Prājāpatya;
this very same [penance], when one eats only as much food as fills the palm of the hand, is the Atikṛcchra.
The Kṛcchrātikṛcchra consists of subsisting on milk for twenty-one days.
A fast for twelve days is proclaimed as the *parāka*.
Eating oil-cake, water from boiled rice, buttermilk, water, and barley meal on successive days,
followed by a fast for one night— this is called the *saumya-kṛcchra*.
By practicing each of these in succession for three nights,
this is to be known as the "Tulāpuruṣa" penance, which lasts for fifteen days.
While performing the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, one should eat morsels of food the size of a peacock’s egg, increasing them according to the growth of the lunar days during the bright fortnight,
and decreasing them by one each day during the dark fortnight.
Alternatively, one may consume two hundred and forty morsels of food in any manner whatsoever within a single month; this is another form of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
One who bathes at the three periods of the day should perform the Kṛcchra penance as well as the Cāndrāyaṇa;
he should mutter purificatory prayers and consecrate the morsels of food with the Gāyatrī mantra.
For sins not specifically prescribed [for atonement], purification is achieved through the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
he who performs this for the sake of dharma attains the same world as the Moon.
One who performs the *kṛcchra* penance while desiring righteousness shall attain great prosperity;
being well-concentrated, he obtains the fruit of a great sacrifice.
Having heard these duties spoken by Yājñavalkya,
the sages spoke thus to that great-souled lord of yogis, who possessed immeasurable splendor:
Those who shall preserve this treatise on Dharma without sloth will attain fame in this world and go to the third heaven.
One desiring knowledge shall obtain knowledge; likewise, one desiring wealth shall obtain wealth;
similarly, one desiring long life shall obtain long life, and one desiring prosperity shall obtain great prosperity.
For whoever shall cause even these three verses to be heard at a śrāddha ceremony, the satisfaction of the ancestors for him shall be inexhaustible; there is no doubt in this matter.
A Brāhmaṇa attains the status of a worthy recipient, a Kṣatriya becomes victorious,
and a Vaiśya becomes possessed of grain and wealth, by the retention of this scripture.
"O Bhagavān, please grant your approval for the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice to belong to that wise man who causes this [text] to be heard by the twice-born on every festival day."
Having heard this speech of the Sage, Yājñavalkya, his soul filled with joy, said,
"So be it," after having paid homage to the Self-Existent One.
[End of the Chapter on Expiation]
The Yājñavalkya-smṛti is completed.
